chapters.title: Set the table
chapters.hook: 1 page can beat a busy morning. What if your first job is not speed, but naming the result?
chapters.counterintuition: A frog is not the task you dislike most, but the task whose result matters most when written down.
chapters.tryThisNow: Within the next 24 hours, the first time a vague task comes up, spend 10 minutes writing a handoff note that names the result and tally each easy task that tries to replace it.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Write the exact result first, then use the seven-step goal method to choose the frog by consequence and start before easy work takes over.

breakdown.fastRead:
Capucine sits in a training class with one blank line on the worksheet: desired result. Everyone wants to talk about tasks first. Email, slides, calls, errands. Then the instructor brings up the Mark Twain frog maxim, and the room sees the snag. You cannot eat the right frog until you know which outcome the frog serves.

A named result makes the frog visible. The goal on the page gives your day a target. Without it, the easiest task can dress up as progress. With it, the list starts to sort itself. The hard task with the largest consequence moves to the front.
breakdown.deepRead:
A written goal turns pressure into a next step. It takes the fog out of work by making the finish line visible. Once the finish line is plain, a task can be judged by consequence. Does it move the result, or does it only make the day feel busy?

Wesley has the Open Library OL27236208M record open beside a paper copy of the 2017 third edition. The phrase he circles is plain: decide exactly. Not vaguely. Not someday. Exactly. He had written "improve sales" on his list. That phrase gave him no frog. Ten minutes later, he writes, "Send the revised proposal to three stalled accounts by Friday." Now the frog has a shape. The first call is still unpleasant, but it is no longer random pain.

The seven-step goal method keeps that clarity from staying dreamy. First the page names the result. Then it records the deadline, the useful actions, the order, the first act, and the daily follow-through. Each step removes a hiding place. A goal in your head can shift to fit your mood. A written goal sits there and asks why the inbox is open.

That is the useful pressure. It is not drama. It is a page with the result, the date, the list, the order, and the first act. Easy work loses some charm when the page says what matters.
breakdown.fullRead:
Maren watches a good student misuse the frog. He picks the chore that feels most annoying, sharpens pencils, and calls it discipline. The class laughs because everyone has done the same thing. Hard work can still matter little. Pain is a poor ranking system.

The Mark Twain image works only after the table is set. The frog is the high-consequence task, not the task with the ugliest feeling. That difference saves the method from becoming self-punishment. If the written result is "finish the grant budget by noon," the frog may be one phone call about a missing number. If the result is "repair the client handoff," the frog may be a clear note that names the next owner.

Open Library OL27236208M points at the same first move in plain language: decide exactly what you want in each area. Each area matters because a person can be busy in one corner while avoiding the result that would change another. A vague work goal, a vague health goal, and a vague money goal all create the same fog. The page has to name the desired result before the task list can tell the truth.

The written-goal worksheet is simple on purpose. Decide exactly what you want. Write it down. Set a deadline. List actions. Organize the list. Act immediately. Do something daily. The order matters. If you list actions before naming the result, the list will fill with familiar chores. If you set no deadline, urgency stays borrowed from other people. If you never act at once, planning becomes a soft place to hide.

The cost is real. Clarity costs the comfort of pretending everything matters. Todd feels it at the kitchen table when his notebook has only three lines left for tomorrow. He wants to keep "research vendors," "clean files," and "answer backlog" because all three sound responsible. The written result says one thing: send the signed renewal packet. Two neat chores have to wait. He gives up the pleasure of a full list and keeps the one task with consequence.

That tradeoff is the point of setting the table. The page does not make work easy. It makes evasion easier to see. A clear result can embarrass a busy morning, since the fifth small task no longer looks like courage. It also gives a fair test for the frog. Ask which task has the largest effect on the result if finished, and the largest cost if delayed.

The method fails when it becomes a decorative list. A page full of noble wishes is not a set table. The result must be plain enough that a stranger could tell whether it happened. The deadline must be real enough to change the order of work. The next action must be small enough to start before confidence arrives.

Mackenzie learns this beside a soccer sideline, where the clipboard has practice drills on one side and a late registration form on the other. Both matter. Only one blocks a family from joining next week. She writes the result at the top: "Submit the final roster tonight." The frog is still awkward. Now it is also obvious.

examples.title: Blank Line Lesson
examples.scenario: Capucine presses her pencil into the worksheet line marked desired result during a Tuesday night planning class. The room is naming errands, calls, and email before anyone names an outcome. When the instructor brings in Mark Twain's frog image, Capucine sees the confusion: the frog is not the ugliest chore on the page. It is the task tied to the result she has not written yet.
examples.whatToDo: Capucine writes the result first, then circles the one task whose delay would hurt that result most. Only then does she let the frog image guide the morning.
examples.whyItMatters: The learning problem is the reader's problem. A concrete result keeps the frog from becoming any task that happens to feel unpleasant.

examples.title: Exactly, Then Friday
examples.scenario: Wesley's first page at the public library says, "get clients moving again," and the list below it sprawls across calls, templates, and reading. The Open Library OL27236208M entry for the 2017 third edition sits beside his notes while he rereads the words decide exactly. A later page says, "Send three revised proposals by Friday." The same calls now fall into order.
examples.whatToDo: Wesley replaces the loose wish with one dated result, then rewrites the list so every item either serves Friday's proposals or leaves the page.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast carries the rule. The list did not get shorter through willpower; it got honest when the result and deadline became plain.

examples.title: Deadline Across the Table
examples.scenario: Paxton says, "The plan is in my head," and Maren slides the written-goal worksheet across the coffee shop counter. "Then where is the deadline?" she asks. Paxton taps the empty box under Set a deadline. The seven steps also ask for a written list and daily action. "And the first action?" He points to another blank.
examples.whatToDo: Paxton fills the deadline box and writes the first action before adding another task. Maren keeps the worksheet on the table until the plan can be seen.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange shows why mental planning is weak. Blank boxes reveal missing parts faster than another promise to remember the plan later.

examples.title: The List Tightens
examples.scenario: Oceane reads the Seven-step goal method at her kitchen table and feels pleased by the long action list. Wait, list actions is only step four. Organize the list comes next. She wants to start with logo tweaks because they are clean. The product page copy is the ugly frog; it carries the sale. Her pen moves it to the top before she can bargain with herself.
examples.whatToDo: Oceane ranks the actions by consequence, not comfort, and moves the product page copy above the cleaner design tasks on the same sheet.
examples.whyItMatters: A list can become another hiding place. Ordering the list forces the reader to see which action carries the result and which ones merely feel tidy.

examples.title: Rosters Before Drills
examples.scenario: Mackenzie has twenty quiet minutes on the soccer sideline before cleats start scraping the path. The clipboard holds drill notes, snack emails, and one roster form that decides whether a new player can join Saturday. Mark Twain's frog image would make the roster the morning's first bite. She ranks the page before any whistle, cone, or message gets touched.
examples.whatToDo: Mackenzie writes the roster result at the top of the clipboard and reserves the first attention for the form that changes Saturday's outcome.
examples.whyItMatters: Consequence, not irritation, identifies the frog. The reader learns to allocate scarce attention before motion makes every task look equally urgent.

examples.title: Packet or Backlog
examples.scenario: Todd sorts the parent volunteer packet at the kitchen table beside the written goal, the deadline, and the ordered list. The packet needs one awkward handoff note before bedtime. The family group chat also has six small requests, and ignoring them will annoy people. He weighs the visible irritation against the missed deadline. The Seven-step goal method says Act immediately, so the packet gets the first sentence.
examples.whatToDo: Todd writes the handoff note for the renewal packet before opening the group chat, then leaves the smaller replies for after the first action is done.
examples.whyItMatters: Starting at once protects the plan from polite delay. The reader sees that clarity still asks for a cost, often the cost of disappointing easy requests.

questions.prompt: Capucine opens her laptop and sees email before the blank result line on her worksheet. Which first response fits Set the table?
choices: Write the goal before choosing which task deserves the first hour.
Open email first because fresh messages can reveal the real priority.
Sort the inbox quickly so the worksheet feels less crowded afterward.
questions.explanation: The goal has to steer the task choice. Email may contain useful items, but starting there lets visible activity pretend to be priority.

questions.prompt: Wesley writes a desired result but leaves the date empty because no client has demanded one. How should he read that gap?
choices: The missing date is fine until someone outside the plan creates pressure.
The open date leaves him free to improve the work without false haste.
The missing date hides urgency, so the goal cannot rank today's actions.
questions.explanation: A deadline exposes urgency before someone else supplies it. Without the date, Wesley's plan can keep favoring comfortable work.

questions.prompt: Paxton says his next moves are clear in his head, but the worksheet has no action list. What should Maren press him to do?
choices: Keep the plan mental for now so the list stays flexible during the week.
Discuss the goal again until the plan feels more inspiring to the team.
Write every action that could help so the plan can be seen and sorted.
questions.explanation: A mental list is easy to bend around mood. Writing the actions gives Paxton material to organize instead of a promise to remember.

questions.prompt: Oceane has twelve useful actions on a page and wants to begin at the top. Which correction matches the seven-step method?
choices: Begin with the first item because writing the list already made the plan concrete.
Spend a separate day thinking about order before any work changes hands.
Organize the list by consequence before treating any item as the first move.
questions.explanation: A list is not yet a plan. Oceane needs order, or the first visible item may beat the action that carries the result.

questions.prompt: Todd finishes the written plan for the renewal packet, then pauses because the first call feels awkward. What action keeps the plan from becoming delay?
choices: Take the first related action now, even if it is only the handoff note.
Wait for confidence so the first action does not damage the quality of the work.
Review the plan tomorrow so the first action has more time to mature.
questions.explanation: The method asks for immediate action after planning. Waiting for confidence gives delay a polished reason to stay in charge.

questions.prompt: Mackenzie blocks one weekly check-in for the roster goal, but the form needs steady progress before Saturday. What change would better fit the method?
choices: Make the weekly check-in longer so the goal receives one serious review.
Do one related action each day so the written goal stays active.
Hold the goal for the weekend when the sideline is quieter.
questions.explanation: Daily action keeps the goal alive after the plan is written. A weekly review can help, but it is too thin as the main follow-through.

questions.prompt: Todd has two unpleasant tasks at the kitchen table: the renewal handoff and a file cleanup. Which test should he use first?
choices: Choose the task that feels most annoying so discomfort cannot win the morning.
Choose the task with the largest consequence for the written result.
Choose the task people will notice first so outside pressure can help.
questions.explanation: The frog is chosen by consequence, not by annoyance. A painful task can still be low value if it does not move the stated result.

questions.prompt: Oceane keeps the product page goal broad because she says a vague target leaves more room for creativity. What is the likely cost?
choices: Easy work can keep looking useful because no written result exposes the mismatch.
Creative work will stop once the result is named and dated on the page.
The task list will become shorter than the project needs by the end of the day.
questions.explanation: Vagueness lets easy work pass as progress. A clear result does not kill creativity; it gives the creative effort a target.

questions.prompt: A colleague tells Capucine that time management should begin by moving faster through small tasks. Which reply best fits Set the table logic?
choices: Speed helps most when the day starts with visible tasks from the inbox.
Clarity comes first because speed cannot fix work aimed at the wrong result.
Small tasks build enough momentum to reveal the main goal by noon.
questions.explanation: Clarity multiplies effort by aiming it. Moving faster through the wrong tasks still leaves the important result untouched.

reviewCards.front: Why does the result need to be written before the task list is ranked?
reviewCards.back: The written result gives every task a consequence test. Without it, easy work can look productive because nothing on the page proves it is off target.

reviewCards.front: How does the Mark Twain frog image help choose the right hard task?
reviewCards.back: It makes the hard, high-consequence task concrete. The frog is not any ugly chore; it is the task that matters most once the desired result is named.

reviewCards.front: What are the seven steps in the written-goal method?
reviewCards.back: Decide exactly what you want; Write it down; Set a deadline; List actions; Organize the list; Act immediately; Do something daily.

reviewCards.front: Why is an action list not enough by itself?
reviewCards.back: A list shows possible moves, but it does not choose priority. The list must be organized so consequence, not comfort or order on the page, decides the first action.

reviewCards.front: What protects planning from becoming another form of delay?
reviewCards.back: Act immediately after the plan is clear. Even a small first move, such as a handoff note, proves the plan is becoming behavior.

reviewCards.front: How should you identify the frog when several tasks feel unpleasant?
reviewCards.back: Choose by consequence. The frog is the task whose completion would help the written result most, and whose delay would cost the most.

implementationPlan.title: Write the Result Note
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Write the Result Note before you rank the day. Name the exact result, set the deadline, list actions, and mark the action with the largest consequence. The note is a handoff from your clear self to your busy self.

ifThenPlans.context: When the day opens with email before a goal is written
ifThenPlans.plan: If the inbox appears first, then Write the Result Note on paper before choosing any task from the messages.

ifThenPlans.context: When a goal has no date attached
ifThenPlans.plan: If the deadline box is blank, then add a date before ranking tasks, even if the date is self-set.

ifThenPlans.context: When the action list is long and busy
ifThenPlans.plan: If the list has more than five actions, then mark the one with the largest consequence and move it to the top.

ifThenPlans.context: When planning feels complete but no work has started
ifThenPlans.plan: If the plan is written, then take one related action at once so the page becomes behavior.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, the first time a vague task appears, Write the Result Note and count how many easy tasks try to claim the first slot before the result is clear.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, keep one index card on your desk labeled Result, Deadline, Frog. Change only that part of your space and watch whether the first task becomes clearer.

memorableLines.text: A named result makes the frog visible.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the chapter's first rule into a portable line.

memorableLines.text: A written goal turns pressure into a next step.
memorableLines.why: It names the mechanism in plain, useful language.

memorableLines.text: Clarity costs the comfort of pretending everything matters.
memorableLines.why: It makes the tradeoff of goal clarity easy to remember.

chapters.title: Plan every day in advance
chapters.hook: Leave the morning unplanned and it fills with everyone else's priorities before you finish your coffee.
chapters.counterintuition: The day becomes freer when it is pinned down: a written list lets you change course without letting every interruption steer.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before you send your next reply, write START on a sticky note beside the screen, then add one line naming the task you will open after the reply.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Plan before pressure: write the day, mark the first hard item, and let monthly, weekly, and master lists feed the page so work begins by choice.

breakdown.fastRead:
Leah expects the short list to make her day feel heavier. Instead, the page gives the day edges. Alan Lakein's old planning maxim works because it turns planning from a nice idea into a work step: if the day is not planned, drift has already been invited.

The useful list is not a memory dump. It is a map for attention. Write the tasks, mark the priority, and let the first hard item meet you before messages do. A plan is a promise made before noise arrives.
breakdown.deepRead:
Ten quiet minutes can save an hour because they move decisions out of the rush. Eric learns this when his daily list sits beside the keyboard before the first reply. The list is plain: three calls, one budget draft, one report section, and two errands. The priority marks change the page. The budget draft gets an A. The errands wait. He is not trying to feel organized; he is removing a small argument from the first work minute.

On Eric's page, loose claims leave his head and sit where his eyes can compare them. Priority marks turn the list from storage into sequence. Then the daily list can pull from the bigger lists: master list for everything, monthly list for what belongs soon, weekly list for this stretch, daily list for what gets done now. A list without order is only a parking lot.

When a client call lands at noon, Eric crosses one item forward and keeps the first priority visible. Changing the page is not failure. The budget draft still has a place. It is how the plan stays alive while the day moves.
breakdown.fullRead:
Agathe's notebook has four pages marked with paper clips. One says Master list. One says Monthly list. One says Weekly list. One says Daily list. The clips look fussy until a new project arrives and nothing has to live in her head. The raw idea goes to the master list. The timing lands on the monthly page. The next few actions move to the weekly page. Tomorrow gets one line, not the whole project.

That is why advance planning is more than writing a lot of tasks. A single daily list can become a junk drawer. It may hold a tax form, a call home, a launch plan, and a lightbulb to buy. The page looks busy, but it gives no order. The four-list hierarchy protects today from carrying every promise at once. It also protects the large promise from vanishing behind small errands.

Alan Lakein's planning rule has force because it is harsh in a useful way. If you do not plan, you are not neutral. You are letting the next sound, the next badge, or the next easy chore make the choice. That does not mean the list is sacred. It means the list gets first claim on your attention before the day starts bidding.

Priority marks are the hinge. Vernon can write fifteen items and still hide from the frog. One mark beside the highest-value task removes that cover. The page now asks for a sequence, not a mood. If the marked item is too large, the next move is to split it into visible steps. Project planning benefits from listing every step first because the hidden step is often where work stalls.

The best small test is visible behavior. Did a task get written? Did one item get ranked above the others? Did a project step move from weekly hope to daily action? If the answer is no, the reader has heard a planning slogan, not used a planning rule. Paper earns its keep when it changes the next minute.

Completion also becomes measurable. Bernard can feel busy after six quick tasks, but the list shows whether the chosen item moved. This matters because work often rewards motion with relief. Crossed-off trivia feels good for a minute. The planned priority is less flattering and more useful. It tells you whether the day served the result you chose.

Follow this rule least when the situation calls for immediate care. A broken pipe, a sick child, or a legal deadline may deserve a direct response before any list is rebuilt. Advance planning governs ordinary work pressure. It should not make you slow to act when delay is the danger. For the usual day, though, write first, rank first, then begin. Revise the page; do not surrender the day.

examples.title: Lakein List Surprise
examples.scenario: Leah copies Alan Lakein's planning maxim on an index card and predicts the card will only scold her. At her office desk, the card sits beside a blank daily list while the inbox fills. By lunch, the surprise is plain: the written list did not trap her. It kept one hard budget draft from being buried under six easy replies.
examples.whatToDo: Leah writes the daily list before opening the inbox, marks the budget draft first, and leaves Lakein's planning card where her hand reaches for the mouse.
examples.whyItMatters: The scene turns a maxim into behavior. Planning has force only when it changes what gets written, marked, protected, or started before drift takes over.

examples.title: Ten-Minute Thread
examples.scenario: Before work, Eric stands by the office coffee counter with his phone in one hand and a blank pad in the other. Eden texts, "Can you check the slide title first?" Eric replies, "Ten minutes. Making the daily list." A moment later: "A is the client draft. B is the slide title. C is receipts." Eden sends back, "Good. Send the draft before the pretty title eats the morning."
examples.whatToDo: Eric spends 10 minutes writing the daily list and adds priority marks before he answers the first request in full.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange shows the list doing its job. It does not collect tasks for comfort; it tells the next message where it belongs in the order.

examples.title: Four-Page Restart
examples.scenario: Vernon begins his usual routine at a library reading table by filling one page until it looks heroic. Then the page swallows a grant proposal, a dentist call, and next month's travel. He stops, turns to four fresh pages, and labels them Master list, Monthly list, Weekly list, Daily list. The grant no longer crowds the dentist call.
examples.whatToDo: Vernon restarts the page: every loose task moves to the right horizon, then only tomorrow's real actions land on the daily list.
examples.whyItMatters: The reset keeps the daily page honest. Longer horizons feed today, but they should not crush today under every unfinished promise.

examples.title: Margin Priority Mark
examples.scenario: Eden's pencil taps once in the margin of a yellow pad. The daily list is only 10 minutes old. Seven lines sit under the date. Beside one line, the priority mark is darker than the words: finish renewal memo. The coffee is still hot, the email tab is still closed, and the page has already made one small demand.
examples.whatToDo: Eden darkens the priority mark beside the renewal memo and places the pad across the keyboard before opening mail.
examples.whyItMatters: The mark turns a list into a sequence. Without it, a neat page can still invite the easiest item to pose as the right one.

examples.title: Friday Evidence Trail
examples.scenario: The handoff failed before Hubert returned the phone call. The evidence was on the pages: the master list held the project name, the monthly list named the week, but the weekly list never gave the daily list a next step. By Friday, the daily page had errands, replies, and no handoff. The missing bridge did the damage.
examples.whatToDo: Hubert adds one next step to the weekly list, copies it onto Monday's daily list, and marks it before smaller replies.
examples.whyItMatters: The review shows why horizons need to connect. A master list can remember a project, but the daily list needs a next action it can execute.

examples.title: Reply Before Repair
examples.scenario: Bernard is halfway through a quick reply when he notices the blank daily list under his wrist. The reply is harmless, but the pattern is not. Yesterday began the same way and the report never moved. He saves the draft, pulls the pad closer, and spends 10 minutes listing the day before the next response writes the order for him.
examples.whatToDo: Bernard saves the reply, writes the daily list, marks the report first, and returns to the message only after the first work block is named.
examples.whyItMatters: The recovery catches the real error while it is still small. Planning before work pressure peaks keeps a useful reply from becoming the day's steering wheel.

questions.prompt: A work log shows four busy mornings and no progress on the budget draft. The only written page was an unmarked task list. Which reading fits best?
choices: The page worked as intended, since capturing everything you did is what a planned day really means.
The page gave some control, but it needed ranking so the hard priority could beat low-value activity.
The page failed mainly because a list should stay mental when the day has many moving parts.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 says a written list increases control, but the control has to serve the harder priority. An equal-weight list can still let easy work lead.

questions.prompt: Two teammates plan a launch day. One writes the list before messages begin; the other waits to see which requests arrive. Which response matches advance planning?
choices: Waiting lets the real interruptions reveal the right order before the list hardens.
Writing early matters only when the day has no urgent outside requests to answer.
Writing early lowers decision friction before fresh requests start bargaining for attention.
questions.explanation: Fact 2 supports planning before work because it reduces decision friction. Waiting for interruptions makes the day's first pressure too powerful.

questions.prompt: A planner has one daily page holding a tax form, a future trip, a project launch, and today's calls. Which change would help first?
choices: Keep the single page, then circle any item that still feels important at midmorning.
Move only the future trip off the page, since travel is the one item not tied to work.
Feed the daily page from master, monthly, and weekly lists so each horizon has a job.
questions.explanation: Fact 3 says longer planning horizons feed the daily list. The fix is not a bigger daily page; it is separating timing before choosing today's actions.

questions.prompt: A list has twelve items, all written with the same weight. Another list has eight items and three priority marks. Which one better guides work?
choices: The twelve-item list, because a fuller inventory gives more control over the day.
The eight-item list, but only because fewer tasks reduce pressure before work starts.
The marked list, because priority marks turn inventory into a sequence for action.
questions.explanation: Fact 4 says priority marks convert a list into a sequence. The number of items matters less than whether the page tells work what comes first.

questions.prompt: Agathe keeps tomorrow's tasks in her head so she can adjust on the fly. By noon, three small chores keep returning to mind. What explains the pattern?
choices: Mental planning is useful, but only when the tasks are equal in value and easy to recall.
Unwritten tasks keep tugging at attention because the mind is still trying to store them.
Small chores repeat because the daily list was made too early to include later details.
questions.explanation: Fact 5 says unwritten tasks keep pulling attention. Writing them down frees the mind to compare and rank them instead of rehearsing them.

questions.prompt: Bernard's marked task is ready, then a client moves a call and two items need new slots. Which conclusion best fits the source rule?
choices: The plan can be revised and still keep its job as the day's guide.
The plan was useful only until the first outside request changed the order.
The plan should now be dropped until the day settles into a clearer pattern.
questions.explanation: Fact 6 says a plan can be revised without being abandoned. A changed call asks for a changed page, not a surrender to drift.

questions.prompt: A morning log shows the first list being made after seven replies, two calls, and a request from a manager. What should the reader infer?
choices: The list is late only if those early messages were less important than the planned work.
The list should have been prepared before execution pressure gave those requests first claim.
The list still works if the reader adds every new request before choosing the priority.
questions.explanation: Fact 7 says the daily list should be prepared before execution pressure peaks. Once replies and calls lead, planning starts behind the day.

questions.prompt: Two project leads open the same messy assignment. Leah lists every step before starting; Eric begins with the most visible step. Which response fits?
choices: Leah fits because project planning benefits from naming every step before action starts.
Eric fits because visible steps reveal the plan faster than a complete written sequence.
Both fit because project work only needs a list after the first obstacle appears.
questions.explanation: Fact 8 says project planning benefits from listing every step first. The visible step can be tempting, but it may hide the real order.

questions.prompt: A worker says the day felt productive, but there is no written record of what was finished. Which answer best follows the list rule?
choices: Working from a list makes completion measurable instead of leaving progress to feeling.
A strong sense of motion is enough when the tasks are familiar and short.
A written record mainly matters when someone else needs proof of the work.
questions.explanation: Fact 9 says working from a list makes completion measurable. Feeling busy can mislead; the list shows whether the chosen work moved.

reviewCards.front: What does advance planning mean before work starts?
reviewCards.back: It means building master, monthly, weekly, and daily lists before action starts, then using the daily page to work from choice rather than impulse.

reviewCards.front: Why are priority marks more than decoration on a daily list?
reviewCards.back: They turn a task inventory into a sequence. The mark tells the reader which item gets first claim, so easy items cannot quietly choose the order.

reviewCards.front: Name the four lists in the planning hierarchy and the job each one does.
reviewCards.back: The master list catches everything. The monthly list sets timing. The weekly list narrows the current stretch. The daily list names today's action.

reviewCards.front: When interruptions change the day, what should happen to the plan?
reviewCards.back: Revise the page and keep using it. The source rule treats changes as part of planning, not as proof that planning was wasted.

reviewCards.front: Recall goal clarity before action (Ch 1): name one concrete moment here where it actually bites.
reviewCards.back: Vernon's four-page restart shows it. The master list holds the project, and the daily list names the next action instead of carrying a vague wish.

reviewCards.front: Why should the daily list be ready before work pressure peaks?
reviewCards.back: Because the first replies, calls, and requests begin bidding for attention. A ready list gives the chosen priority a place before the scramble starts.

implementationPlan.title: Mark Tomorrow's First Line
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice turning a list into a first action before pressure arrives. Write the day's tasks, mark the one that matters most, and keep the mark visible when replies begin. The reader tool is Mark Tomorrow's First Line: one written line that names the next task before the next message pulls you away.

ifThenPlans.context: A reply asks for a quick answer before the day is planned.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the next reply appears before the daily list is written, then write one START line on paper before sending the response.

ifThenPlans.context: The list is full but every item has the same weight.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the page looks busy but flat, then add one priority mark before doing any small item.

ifThenPlans.context: A new interruption makes the old order impossible.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the day changes, then move one item on the page and keep the marked task visible.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next 24 hours, put the word START on a sticky note, notebook margin, or phone wallpaper. Before you send your next response, write one line naming the priority you will open afterward.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of this week, look back once at your lists. Name what changed about planning before pressure: the first task, the number of rewritten items, or how quickly you began.

memorableLines.text: A plan is a promise made before noise arrives.
memorableLines.why: It makes the timing rule short enough to carry into a busy morning.

memorableLines.text: A list without order is only a parking lot.

chapters.title: Apply the 80/20 rule to everything
chapters.hook: 10 lines on a pad can hide the 2 that decide the week.
chapters.counterintuition: What looks like a fair task list is actually a trap when the small jobs get first choice.
chapters.tryThisNow: Next quick-win pull, sit where you work. Move the list under your hand and pre-write: "I start the highest-consequence task first."
chapters.keyTakeaway: Rank tasks by consequence first; the Vital few get prime attention before quick work steals the day.

breakdown.fastRead:
Valerie and Pascal face the same 10-task sheet at a conference room table. Valerie circles the 2 jobs tied to the week's result. Pascal starts with the eight smaller jobs because they will fall fast. By lunch, Pascal has more checks. Valerie has moved the work that matters.

The 80/20 rule says results are uneven. Vilfredo Pareto is tied to the rule because many inputs matter a little, while a few matter a lot. On a task list, those few are the Vital few. The many smaller items are the Trivial many.

Checked boxes can hide a wasted day. Before you begin, ask which task changes money, risk, a kept word, skill, or duty if it gets done. That task gets your first real attention. The small jobs can wait their turn.
breakdown.deepRead:
Every task line takes the same space on paper, so the list lies by looking neat. A one-line errand and a client decision both sit in the same black ink. The 80/20 rule tells you to stop reading the list as equal rows. Read it as consequence.

Bonnie hears this mistake in a training room before a work sprint. A teammate wants to refill forms, sort the queue notes, and answer the easiest callbacks before touching the hard file. Bonnie turns the page sideways and says, "Fast is not the same as first." The sentence works because both choices are real work. One choice only feels safer.

Quick wins are tempting because they end cleanly. You get a small proof that you are busy. The danger is not the small job itself. The danger is letting relief choose the order. Ease is a poor judge of worth.

A hard high-value task can outrank several easy ones. If the high-value item is too large, start the first visible piece. Open the file. Draft the first paragraph. Make the first call. The first move should be plain enough that delay has fewer places to hide.
breakdown.fullRead:
Madeline sits in an onboarding class while the instructor writes Vital few on one side of the board and Trivial many on the other. She frowns because the words sound unfair. The instructor does not call the smaller jobs worthless. He puts 10 tasks under the headings and asks which 2 would change the week.

That is the plain test. The 80/20 rule asks you to judge value before you spend effort. A few customers may bring most revenue. A few projects may shape the year. A few skills may raise the value of every later hour. The rule is not a praise song for busyness. It asks where the work will land.

Use a visible mark. Write the list. Put a V beside the one or two tasks with the largest consequence. If the V task is uncomfortable, do not treat that as proof against it. Hardness may be the reason you keep cleaning around it.

Quick wins still have a place. A tiny chore can warm up your hand. A minor call can keep faith with another person. But quick work becomes trouble when it protects you from the important task. Sorting files can look noble while the real result sits closed.

The Vital few deserve the first chair. Give them the cleanest block of attention, not the crumbs after the day has been picked over. If the important work is large, start one piece that can be seen. Move the folder. Write the first sentence. Dial the first number.

Romain changes his task rack at a community center hall before volunteers arrive. Last week the donation labels sat at eye level and the donor pickup calls hid behind a stack of hangers. This week he pins the pickup calls in front. The rack is no shorter, but his hand reaches for the work with consequence first.

Cedric makes the same move on a phone call with a client proposal. He wants to finish three small edits before the proposal draft. Then he asks which item would still matter if the afternoon collapsed. The proposal opens. The edits wait. Value has to be judged while choice is still alive.

The rule can be misused by people who want a shortcut more than judgment. If Aspen calls a task trivial only because it is dull, she is hiding preference inside math. Ask what changes if the task is finished. Money, danger, a kept promise, a skill, or a duty are stronger clues than mood.

This rule fails the emergency dispatcher, the nurse in triage, and anyone whose whole list carries live, equal-risk duties. For those roles, private ranking can do harm. The 80/20 rule fits a normal workday with discretion, where some tasks plainly carry more consequence than others. Equal treatment can be delay in tidy clothes.

examples.title: Two Copies of 10 Tasks
examples.scenario: Two copies of the same 10-task sheet land on a conference room table. Valerie circles the two high-value tasks and pulls the budget memo close. Pascal starts with the eight minor tasks because they will fall fast. At noon, Pascal has more checks, but Valerie has moved the work with the combined value.
examples.whatToDo: Valerie ranks the 10 tasks by consequence, then moves the two high-value items to the top of the page.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast shows why counting completions can mislead. A reader needs to ask which two tasks carry the value of the other eight.

examples.title: Fast Is Not First
examples.scenario: Before a Monday task sprint at a community center hall, peer coach Bonnie watches a teammate stack minor chores beside an important task. The quick wins promise visible completion and a safer mood. Bonnie turns the list sideways and says, "Fast is not the same as first." The teammate has to rank the important task before the easy stack cleans up the morning.
examples.whatToDo: Bonnie has the teammate mark the important file with a V and push the quick-win stack below it.
examples.whyItMatters: Quick wins are tempting because they finish cleanly. The coaching move separates relief from real priority.

examples.title: Pareto on the Board
examples.scenario: In an onboarding classroom, Madeline studies a worksheet with customers, projects, skills, and duties in even rows. The instructor writes Vilfredo Pareto, 80/20, Vital few, and Trivial many on the board. Madeline keeps counting rows until the exercise asks which few would move most of the result.
examples.whatToDo: Madeline sorts the worksheet into Vital few and Trivial many, then names why equal rows can carry unequal value.
examples.whyItMatters: The class setting makes uneven distribution visible. The reader sees why a neat list still needs a consequence test.

examples.title: The Rack Reordered
examples.scenario: Last week, Romain cleared the community center task rack from left to right: labels, supply slips, small signs, then the donor pickup calls he never reached. This morning he changes one cue. The two calls with the largest consequence sit at eye level. The rack is not shorter, but his first reach has changed.
examples.whatToDo: Romain puts the two highest-consequence responsibilities at eye level before the small chores can claim the shift.
examples.whyItMatters: The same list behaves differently when placement favors value. A reader can move one object before effort starts.

examples.title: Before Effort Goes
examples.scenario:
"I can finish three small edits before the proposal," Cedric says on the phone.

"Will those edits change the week?"

"They will make the list shorter."

"Shorter is not the same test. Which task would still matter if your afternoon collapsed?"

Cedric touches the proposal file and leaves the edits closed.
examples.whatToDo: Cedric judges value before spending effort, then opens the proposal while the easy edits remain untouched.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange keeps value from being guessed after the fact. The reader sees the choice while it can still change the day.

examples.title: The Work Mask
examples.scenario: Aspen's task list sits beside a mug at the kitchen table: vendor terms, renewal call, file low-value receipts. Receipts would be small work. She could finish the stack and feel decent. But the renewal call is the important task with consequence. Her mind keeps sliding away from the phone. That slide is the tell.
examples.whatToDo: Aspen leaves the receipts in place, writes the first sentence for the renewal call, and dials before minor work absorbs the morning.
examples.whyItMatters: Avoidance often looks productive from the outside. Naming the slide helps the reader start the high-value task first.

questions.prompt: Two team leads finish Friday with different evidence. One has nine small checks; one has the client decision finished. Which judgment fits the 80/20 rule?
choices: Treat the nine checks as the stronger day because more lines closed.
Treat the neatest list as the stronger day because motion stayed visible.
Treat the client decision as stronger because consequence outranks count.
questions.explanation: The source fact tests consequence, not count. A full checklist can still miss the task that changes the result.

questions.prompt: A work log lists 10 tasks. Two drive most of the week's result, while eight keep the surface neat. Which first move fits the 80/20 rule?
choices: Divide attention across all 10 tasks so the plan looks balanced.
Clear the eight upkeep tasks so the list gains early motion.
Protect the two result-driving tasks before the day gets spent.
questions.explanation: The fact says a minority of tasks can carry most results. Equal attention would treat uneven value as if it were even.

questions.prompt: At the community center hall, Bonnie sees three quick chores beside one hard file before a task sprint. The chores would be done in minutes. How should she read the pull?
choices: The quick chores are attractive because they finish fast, so she should test their consequence.
The quick chores are the best start because visible progress can warm up the day.
The quick chores are the safest priority because speed shows where energy should go.
questions.explanation: Low-value tasks tempt because they finish quickly. The fix is to test consequence before speed chooses the order.

questions.prompt: Pascal opens his laptop with a hard analysis and six small inbox items waiting. He wants the inbox gone first. Which next move matches the residue warning?
choices: Wait for the inbox to shrink, then begin the larger analysis.
Use the early stretch to make the whole list look lighter.
Start the high-value analysis before leftover work fills the day.
questions.explanation: Starting with high value protects the day from residue. Small items can consume the room the important task needed.

questions.prompt: Madeline's practice sheet includes customers, projects, skills, and duties. Which use of 80/20 matches the broader lesson?
choices: Apply it across customers, projects, skills, and duties when value is uneven.
Keep it for sales figures where the uneven pattern is easiest to count.
Use it only for customer lists and leave daily responsibilities outside it.
questions.explanation: The source names customers, projects, skills, and responsibilities. Treating 80/20 as sales-only is too narrow.

questions.prompt: Romain sees one hard duty with a large result and several easy duties with small results. Which ranking follows the rule?
choices: Let several easy duties add up until they outrank the hard one.
Put the hard high-value duty above the easy low-value duties.
Give the easy duties first place because there are more of them.
questions.explanation: The fact says a hard high-value task should outrank several easy low-value tasks. Number and comfort are weaker clues.

questions.prompt: Aspen keeps filing receipts while the renewal call waits on the table. What should she notice about that work?
choices: Useful-looking minor work may be avoidance when it protects delay.
Work-related filing is harmless because it still clears something.
A full table of small work proves the morning is being used well.
questions.explanation: Avoidance can hide inside real work. The filing is not harmless if it keeps the consequence task untouched.

questions.prompt: Cedric learns after lunch that three finished edits changed little, while the unstarted proposal carried the result. What should change tomorrow?
choices: Use finished effort afterward to decide which task deserved the time.
Judge value before spending effort, while the choice can still move.
Let the number of completed edits reveal the strongest task later.
questions.explanation: Value has to be judged before effort is spent. Looking back after the work is done cannot protect the priority.

questions.prompt: Valerie has a loud request, a quick errand, and one Vital few task at the start of the morning. Where should prime attention go?
choices: Give it to the loud request because urgency has already announced itself.
Give it to the Vital few task before noise and ease take over.
Give it to the quick errand because a fast finish clears space.
questions.explanation: Prime attention belongs to the Vital few. Loudness and speed can feel urgent without proving consequence.

reviewCards.front: Which matters more in this task-list situation - goal clarity before action (Ch 1) or the 80/20 rule - and why?
reviewCards.back: Goal clarity names the result first. The 80/20 rule takes over once the list exists: choose the few tasks with the largest consequence before easy work gets the day.

reviewCards.front: What does Vilfredo Pareto's 80/20 rule ask you to see on a task list?
reviewCards.back: It asks you to see uneven value. A few tasks may produce most of the result while many other tasks keep the surface neat.

reviewCards.front: Why can quick wins be risky when an important task is waiting?
reviewCards.back: Quick wins finish cleanly, so they offer relief and visible proof. They become risky when that relief lets the important task stay untouched.

reviewCards.front: What are the two named parts of the Pareto principle framework used here?
reviewCards.back: Vilfredo Pareto's 80/20 framework names the Vital few and the Trivial many. Uneven distribution is why the Vital few get prime attention.

reviewCards.front: Who can be misled by the 80/20 rule?
reviewCards.back: It can mislead people whose duties carry live, equal risk, such as emergency dispatchers or triage nurses. The rule fits workdays where tasks clearly differ in consequence.

implementationPlan.title: Mark the Vital Few
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice marking the Vital few before effort starts. Write the list, put a V beside the one or two tasks with the largest consequence, then move the marked page where your hand reaches first.

ifThenPlans.context: The next time quick wins make minor chores feel attractive
ifThenPlans.plan: Move the minor chores below the marked V and pre-write, "Visible completion waits until the important task starts."

ifThenPlans.context: The next time a loud request tries to take the first block
ifThenPlans.plan: Put the marked V in front of the request and pre-write, "I can handle this after the high-value task starts."

ifThenPlans.context: The next time small chores start looking safer than the hard task
ifThenPlans.plan: Place the hard-task file on top of the list and pre-write the first sentence you will use to begin.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next 24 hours, the next time quick wins pull, move one easy item below your marked V and pre-write the exact refusal you will say to yourself.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, tally each time you choose a quick win before a marked V task. At week's end, read the number and choose one placement change for the next list.

memorableLines.why: It compresses the danger of counting completions instead of consequence.

memorableLines.why: It gives the reader a compact test for quick-win temptation.

chapters.title: Consider the consequences
chapters.hook: Which task changes your next month, and which one only quiets your next ten minutes?
chapters.counterintuition: A quiet proposal can lack deadline pressure and still outrank every pinging message. The later result may be larger than the noise beside it.
chapters.tryThisNow: At your next task handoff, touch the laptop lid and spend ten minutes marking one checklist item with the largest later consequence.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Rank tasks by what they change later, not by how loudly they press now; mark the highest-consequence item before small relief spends the day.

breakdown.fastRead:
Iris has the proposal open on the coffee table, but the phone keeps offering easier wins. A message can be answered, cleared, and forgotten. The proposal will not give that quick relief, yet it may change the long-term result of the week.

That is the rule: consequence is a priority signal. The task with the larger future impact deserves first claim on attention, even when another task feels smoother. Relief is not rank. Before work begins, ask what this action will still matter to later.
breakdown.deepRead:
Consequence thinking works because it moves the contest out of the mood of the moment. Messages feel important because they flash, buzz, and make a small social debt visible. A proposal feels quiet because its reward sits farther away. The test asks which result will still be felt after the inbox is clean.

Lucas and Greta use the test in the stockroom while a delivery cart waits by the back door. Lucas says, "The shelves are messy." Greta taps the clipboard and asks, "Which activity has highest value?" Lucas points to the vendor call only he can make. Greta asks the next part: "What can only I do?" He laughs, because three other people can stack boxes. Nobody else can close the call. The last question lands harder: "What is the most valuable use of time now?" The cart still waits, but the call moves first.

The full framework has four parts. Ask "What are the potential consequences?", "Which activity has highest value?", "What can only I do?", and "What is the most valuable use of time now?" These are not slogans. They force a mark on the page. Future consequence gives priority its teeth. Once the mark is visible, busy work has to argue for its place.
breakdown.fullRead:
Frances reads two drafts on the ferry deck: a short answer to a harmless message and a rough opening for the proposal. The message would make her feel caught up before the boat docks. The rough opening would make the proposal real enough to finish. Both are work, but they do not carry the same aftereffect.

The danger is treating consequence thinking like a grand mood. A person can say "long-term perspective" and still keep choosing the cleanest small task. The useful version changes the next visible move. One line gets circled. One task gets delayed. One low-consequence yes gets turned down before it steals the hour.

That is why the mark matters. A tick beside the highest-consequence item is small, almost dull, but it breaks the trance of present comfort. Layla sees this after a call ends and her hand reaches for the message list. She pauses at the laptop lid, writes three tasks, and puts a check beside the one with the largest future impact. Then she starts the checked task before the quick replies can make the day look productive.

Long-term perspective does not mean every hard task wins. It means the result has to be examined before comfort votes. An uncomfortable task may be pointless. A simple task may matter because it protects a later opening. Consequence, not discomfort, does the ranking.

The short-term relief trap is tempting because it gives proof of motion. The sent reply, the cleared notice, the tiny favor accepted, and the quick errand all feel like evidence. Yet each one spends time that cannot go to the task only the reader can do. A low-consequence yes is still a yes. It writes a claim on the day.

The counter-case keeps the rule honest. If Greta sees a customer order about to ship with the wrong address, the proposal should wait. That small fix has a real consequence now: the package goes to the right place, the customer avoids a bad day, and the team avoids repair work. Obeying "largest long-term task first" would be a mistake in that moment. The better rule is sharper: choose the action whose consequence is largest after the real costs are counted.

This is why the mark comes before the work, not after. It does not worship size, pain, or distance. It asks for the real aftereffect. Sometimes that is the proposal. Sometimes it is the small fix that prevents a larger mess. Either way, the future gets a vote before the easy task takes the chair.

examples.title: Proposal Beside Messages
examples.scenario: The proposal packet lies open on Iris's coffee table, and four messages keep lighting the phone beside it. One path gives short-term relief: answer each message and feel caught up. The other starts the proposal that may change the long-term result of the week. Iris weighs the clean inbox against the work that could still matter Friday.
examples.whatToDo: Iris writes both options on a pad, checks the proposal as the larger consequence, and leaves the messages until the first proposal paragraph exists.
examples.whyItMatters: The scene separates relief from rank. A reader can copy the mark before messages make small comfort look like the day's real priority.

examples.title: Stockroom Three Questions
examples.scenario: Before the store opens, shift lead Lucas stands in the retail stockroom with one hand on the delivery cart. "Boxes first?" he asks. Greta points to the vendor number clipped to his board. "Which activity has highest value?" Lucas says the call. "What can only I do?" The boxes stay loud, but the three questions move the call to the front.
examples.whatToDo: Lucas circles the vendor call, asks Greta to start the boxes, and makes the call before the stockroom noise can choose for him.
examples.whyItMatters: The three questions turn a noisy room into a ranked list. They help the reader find the task that cannot be handed off just because it is less visible.

examples.title: Gym Sign-Up Surprise
examples.scenario: Levi expects the school gymnasium sign-up sheet to make the answer obvious. The snack table needs labels, and thirty parents will notice. Then the principal asks who will draft the sponsor proposal before noon. The labels would get applause tonight; the proposal could open next month's opportunity. The long-time perspective changes the priority.
examples.whatToDo: Levi hands the labels to a volunteer, writes the sponsor proposal first, and lets future impact outrank the task with the easier audience.
examples.whyItMatters: The reveal shows why present attention can mislead. The most noticed task is not always the one that protects tomorrow's opportunity.

examples.title: Draft Thread Pause
examples.scenario:
Frances saves a draft message before sending it.
Desmond: "Inbox clear?"
Frances: "Almost. Proposal untouched."
Desmond: "Which one changes Friday?"
Frances: "Proposal. The message just lowers the buzz."
Desmond: "Then mark that one."
The saved draft waits while the long-term result gets the next line.
examples.whatToDo: Frances leaves the draft unsent, puts a check beside the proposal opening, and writes the first useful line before returning to the thread.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange makes the trap easy to hear. A reply can feel clean while the result that matters later remains untouched.

examples.title: Ferry Lid Reset
examples.scenario: After a client call on the ferry deck, Layla's hand goes to the laptop lid the way it always does before messages. She stops with the lid half open. On a sticky note she writes the three questions, checks the highest value task, and names the best use now before the message list can set the next hour.
examples.whatToDo: Layla restarts the transition by touching the laptop lid, checking the highest-value task, and opening that file instead of the message list.
examples.whyItMatters: The pause makes the tool usable in a normal work seam. The reader gets a habit-stack cue rather than another vague promise to focus.

examples.title: Lift Line Notebook
examples.scenario: Saturday morning at the resort base, analyst Desmond waits in the ski lift line with his notebook resting on one glove. Three tasks sit in pencil beside a paper cup. He adds a small check beside the client outline with the biggest future impact. The long-time perspective is not dramatic; it is a dark mark beside the opportunity that would otherwise wait.
examples.whatToDo: Desmond keeps the checked outline at the top of the notebook and starts it when he opens his laptop after the wait.
examples.whyItMatters: A small mark can carry the priority when the setting changes. The reader sees that consequence thinking becomes useful only when it changes the next file opened.

questions.prompt: Iris's task list shows one proposal that could affect next month and six messages that would be easy to clear. Which first mark fits the consequence test?
choices: Mark the messages first if their pressure makes them harder to ignore.
Mark the proposal first if its future result is larger than the reply relief.
Mark the most unpleasant item first if discomfort proves it carries weight.
questions.explanation: Future consequence is the priority signal. The proposal earns the mark through later impact, not through discomfort or message pressure.

questions.prompt: Two leads see the same busy morning: Lucas asks what will still matter next week, while Levi starts with the loudest request. Which response fits the consequence test?
choices: Lucas's response fits because long-term thinking improves the short-term choice.
Levi's response fits because pressure is the clearest sign of importance.
Both responses fit because any fast start reduces the cost of delay.
questions.explanation: Long-term thinking guides the near-term move. Loud pressure can be a trap when it hides the larger result.

questions.prompt: Before the store opens, three people can stack boxes in the stockroom, but only Lucas can close the vendor call. How should he rank the work?
choices: He should stack boxes first if they are quick enough to clear before the call.
He should split his attention so the visible room and the call both move.
He should take the vendor call first because it is the task only he can do.
questions.explanation: The only-I-can-do question changes the ranking. Quick delegable work can wait when a higher-value task depends on Lucas.

questions.prompt: A note beside Frances's laptop lists a simple reply, a half-done form, and a hard proposal opening. Which cue should decide the best use now?
choices: Choose by the task with the largest consequence, even if another task is easier to start.
Choose by the task already half finished, since momentum protects the rest of the day.
Choose by the reply, since a clean thread gives the next task more room.
questions.explanation: Best use changes with consequence, not convenience. Ease and momentum can help, but they do not outrank the larger result.

questions.prompt: Layla's proposal has no one asking about it yet, while small requests keep arriving. What should she infer before she starts answering?
choices: The proposal can wait because important work usually announces itself through urgency.
The proposal may be important even before it becomes urgent or visible to others.
The small requests should be cleared first so future work has less friction.
questions.explanation: Important work may be quiet at first. Waiting for urgency lets small requests crowd the task before its consequence becomes visible.

questions.prompt: A message log shows eight one-minute replies before lunch and no progress on Desmond's client outline. Which reading is most useful?
choices: The replies were harmless because no single message took enough time to matter.
The replies proved the client outline was not urgent enough to protect.
The replies crowded out a larger future gain even though each one looked small.
questions.explanation: Small urgent tasks can still consume the space for a larger gain. The trap is judging each reply alone instead of the outline it displaced.

questions.prompt: Greta asks Lucas for a quick favor that will not affect the vendor outcome. What consequence-minded answer should Lucas give?
choices: He should decline or delay it because a low-consequence yes spends time the vendor call needs.
He should accept it because small yeses preserve flexibility during a busy shift.
He should accept it if the favor takes less time than explaining why it can wait.
questions.explanation: A low-consequence yes still claims time. Lucas protects the higher-consequence call instead of preserving every small opening.

questions.prompt: Two coworkers sort tasks after a long day: one ranks consequences before starting, and one judges them after fatigue sets in. Which habit fits the consequence rule?
choices: The after-work review fits because completed tasks reveal their real value.
The before-start ranking fits because consequence should guide the first move.
Both habits fit because any review can correct the next day's task order.
questions.explanation: Consequence belongs before the start, when it can change behavior. After fatigue arrives, the day has already been spent.

questions.prompt: Frances dislikes the proposal opening and enjoys clearing replies. Which reason would justify starting the proposal anyway?
choices: Discomfort alone proves the proposal is the right frog for the day.
Enjoyment alone proves the replies are too easy to count as real work.
Long-term value can make the proposal worth starting despite discomfort.
questions.explanation: Immediate discomfort is not the test by itself. Long-term value is what can justify doing the harder task before the easier relief.

reviewCards.front: How does long-term consequence change a task list?
reviewCards.back: It asks what will happen later if each task is done, delayed, or ignored. The item with the larger future impact moves up, even when a smaller task feels cleaner now.

reviewCards.front: How do the three questions expose highest value, only I can do, and best use now?
reviewCards.back: They ask which activity has highest value, what only I can do, and what is the most valuable use of time now. Add potential consequences before the three questions when the stakes are unclear.

reviewCards.front: Why can messages fool a person into picking the wrong first task?
reviewCards.back: Messages offer short-term relief and visible closure. The proposal may feel worse in the moment, but its long-term result can make it the true first task.

reviewCards.front: When does the only-I-can-do question change the order of work?
reviewCards.back: It changes the order when a high-value task depends on one person's action and the other tasks can be handled by someone else, even if those tasks are quicker.

reviewCards.front: How would you restate goal clarity before action (Ch 1), then use it on consequence ranking?
reviewCards.back: Goal clarity names the wanted result before tasks are chosen. Here it helps define the result first, then use long-term consequence to mark the task that serves it best.

reviewCards.front: How can one-minute tasks still damage the day?
reviewCards.back: Each task may look harmless alone, but together they can crowd out a large future gain. The cost is the proposal, call, or outline that never gets started.

implementationPlan.title: Mark the Consequence Check
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice marking the task whose result will matter later. Use the consequence questions before comfort chooses for you. The visible check is the tool: it turns long-term perspective into the next file opened, call made, or yes delayed.

ifThenPlans.context: When a task handoff leaves you between two pieces of work
ifThenPlans.plan: If you are between tasks, then touch the laptop lid or doorknob and mark the highest-consequence item before opening messages.

ifThenPlans.context: When a quick task could be done by someone else
ifThenPlans.plan: If the quick task is delegable, then ask what only you can do and check that task before helping with the easier work.

ifThenPlans.context: When a low-consequence yes would feel polite
ifThenPlans.plan: If the yes would steal time from a higher-consequence task, then delay or decline it in one plain sentence.

ifThenPlans.context: When tiny urgent tasks begin to stack up
ifThenPlans.plan: If small requests start piling up, then mark the large future gain they would crowd out and start that item first.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next 24 hours, at each task handoff, touch an object you already use and mark one checklist item with the largest later consequence.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, swap first-message clearing for a first consequence mark. Compare the first half and second half of the week by which important task moved sooner.

memorableLines.why: It makes priority feel like a test rather than a mood.

memorableLines.why: It turns a small agreement into a visible cost.

chapters.title: Practice creative procrastination
chapters.hook: You want the whole list done. What if one unfinished chore is the door to the real frog?
chapters.counterintuition: Despite the guilt that follows an unfinished list, some tasks earn their place by being delayed. Creative procrastination protects high-value work by naming what you will Stop, Postpone, Delegate, or Eliminate.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before you start your next work block, clear one low-value item from your desk or screen, place the frog in front of you, and rehearse one polite no.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Creative procrastination means choosing low-value work to stop, postpone, delegate, or eliminate before it steals the best hour from your real priority.

breakdown.fastRead:
Florent is halfway through polishing a neat status note when the proposal folder bumps his wrist. The note is almost done. The proposal carries the consequence. He catches the error while the easy work still feels useful, writes status note on a posteriorities list, and puts the proposal in the center of the table.

This tool means delay by choice, not by drift. A posteriorities list is a stop list. It names work to Stop, Postpone, Delegate, or leave behind so the frog has room.

A stop list guards the hour your frog needs. Use the same care on what you will not do as you use on what you will do. The priority list names the frog. The posteriorities list clears the table.
breakdown.deepRead:
Every yes spends attention before it spends time. A small task can take the first clean hour, then leave the hard task with scraps. The danger is that low-value work often looks tidy, polite, and nearly finished.

Zachary catches the trap in a memo before the weekly review. He writes, "Knowing what I know now, I would not start the vendor update again as a weekly slide deck. I will stop the duplicate chart, postpone the color pass, delegate the raw notes, and eliminate the meeting copy." The memo works because it turns guilt into four visible choices.

Zero-based thinking is the test inside that memo. It asks whether you would start the task today, knowing what you know now. If the answer is no, old effort does not get a fresh claim on tomorrow.

Old effort does not own tomorrow's hour. That sentence is strict. A stale task may have been useful once and still be wrong now. The polite no belongs here too. Saying no to a low-value request is not rude when a real priority already has the slot.

A polite no keeps a hidden yes off the calendar. The words can be short: "I cannot take that on this week." The strength comes from the protected work behind the sentence, not from a long defense.
breakdown.fullRead:
Willow and Carmen split one crowded morning in opposite directions. Willow opens the hard client draft first, then writes a second list beside it: stop the duplicate report, postpone the formatting pass, delegate the data pull, eliminate the meeting that repeats the email. Carmen answers each small request as it arrives. By lunch, Carmen has five tidy wins and no draft. Willow has one rough draft and a table with fewer traps on it.

That split is the whole chapter in plain clothes. The better worker is not the person who finishes more items. The better worker protects the item with the strongest consequence.

Low-value work can wear a responsible costume. It feels good to finish a small thing. It feels kind to say yes. It feels loyal to keep a routine because the team once spent time building it. Creative procrastination asks for a harder question: what happens if this task gets another hour?

Douglas brings that question to a peer review call. He taps an old routine checklist and writes zero-based thinking at the top. "We have always done this," he says. His coach does not argue about the past. She says, "Would you buy this hour again today?" The room changes. Douglas is no longer defending yesterday's work. He is deciding whether tomorrow's time should pay for it.

The answer can lead to four moves. Stop means the work ends. Postpone means it waits behind higher-value work. Delegate means someone else handles it because your own touch adds little value. Eliminate means the task leaves the system instead of moving to next week. These words are plain because the behavior must be plain. You can see each one on a calendar, in an inbox, or on a page.

Nova learns the same rule in an onboarding class. The instructor hands out two sheets. The first is a priority list. The second is blank and titled posteriorities. Nova fills the first sheet fast, then freezes at the second. She has never been asked to name what she will refuse. That confusion is useful. It shows the gap between wanting focus and making room for it.

The polite no closes that gap. Nova practices one sentence from the role-play card: "I am not available for that this week." She leaves the priority block visible on the classroom calendar. The no is not a speech. It is a clean fence around work that already matters more.

Pushed too far, creative procrastination curdles into avoidance. Marshall sees this on Monday when he puts a hard customer call on his stop list and calls it discipline. By Thursday, he writes the real result on paper: keep the account. The call is the frog. The tidy side work belongs on the posteriorities list, not the difficult conversation.

So the standard stays tight. Delay low-value work on purpose. Do not delay high-value work because it feels heavy. Creative procrastination is honest only after you know which task carries the biggest consequence. Once that is clear, the unfinished low-value task is not a failure. It is the space your real work needed.

examples.title: Florent Stops the Status Note
examples.scenario: Florent is checking commas on a status note at the status-note desk when the proposal folder slides under his wrist. The note is nearly finished, which makes the error feel harmless. He spots the priority list beside his coffee, writes status note under posteriorities, marks it stop doing, and protects the proposal hour.
examples.whatToDo: Florent closes the status draft, writes it on the posteriorities list, and puts the proposal folder where the note had been.
examples.whyItMatters: The recovery happens in the tempting middle, not after the damage is done. Low-value work often wins because it is almost finished.

examples.title: Zachary Sends the Fresh-Start Memo
examples.scenario: Inside the decision memo, operations lead Zachary starts the weekly review packet with one question: "Knowing what I know now, I would not restart the vendor update as a slide deck. I will stop the duplicate chart, postpone the color pass, delegate the raw notes, and eliminate the meeting copy." The document makes zero-based thinking visible.
examples.whatToDo: Zachary sends the memo, removes the duplicate meeting from the packet, and asks for a fresh yes before the deck gets another week.
examples.whyItMatters: A written zero-based test keeps old effort from bullying the calendar. The task has to earn new time, not live forever because it once began.

examples.title: Willow and Carmen Split the Morning
examples.scenario: The team calendar fills before lunch. Willow marks one client draft as high consequence and moves two tidy chores to a stop list. Carmen answers every small request as it lands, then reaches the draft with ten minutes left. Willow has a rough draft. Carmen has five inbox wins and no frog touched.
examples.whatToDo: Willow names the client draft first, then lets the posteriorities list hold the small chores until the draft has a real start.
examples.whyItMatters: Selective neglect beats accidental drift. Without a visible no-list, trivial work can look like progress while it wins the day by default.

examples.title: Douglas Tests the Old Routine
examples.scenario: "We have always done this," Douglas says on the peer review call, tapping the old routine checklist. He writes zero-based thinking at the top before the coach asks, "Would you buy this hour again today?" Douglas circles the weekly review and hears the stale commitment lose its borrowed authority.
examples.whatToDo: Douglas runs the zero-based question on the checklist and cuts the duplicate prep instead of defending the old routine.
examples.whyItMatters: The reframe changes the unit of judgment. Past effort may deserve respect, but future time still needs a fresh reason.

examples.title: Nova Practices the Polite No
examples.scenario: In the onboarding classroom, Nova reads the role-play card twice. A teammate asks her to take a low-value report this week. Nova starts writing a long apology, then the instructor points to the calendar grid. Her confusion becomes the lesson: a polite no protects the priority already living in that slot.
examples.whatToDo: Nova says, "I cannot take that on this week," then leaves the priority block visible on the classroom calendar.
examples.whyItMatters: A clear no prevents a hidden yes from landing on the calendar. The boundary works because it is brief, respectful, and tied to real capacity.

examples.title: Marshall Repairs the Stop List
examples.scenario: On Monday at the customer follow-up desk, Marshall put the hard customer call on his stop list and called the move creative procrastination. By Thursday, the same desk holds a written result: keep the account. He sees the call is high-value work and moves only the tidy side work off the morning.
examples.whatToDo: Marshall writes the desired result first, keeps the customer call on the priority list, and shifts only low-value side work to posteriorities.
examples.whyItMatters: Creative procrastination needs a clear priority before it can be honest. Otherwise the tool becomes a nicer name for avoiding the frog.

questions.prompt: Two reports sit half-finished: one shapes a client decision, and one is a tidy internal recap. Which next move fits creative procrastination?
choices: Check which report carries the stronger consequence, then leave the weaker one unfinished for now.
Finish both reports in the order they were started, then judge their value after completion.
Complete the internal recap first because quick completion builds discipline for harder work.
questions.explanation: The source fact says not everything deserves completion. The keyed move uses consequence to decide what can stay unfinished; the near misses treat completion itself as discipline.

questions.prompt: A planning sheet lists ten priorities, but the margins have no space for tasks to stop, wait, move, or leave. What is missing?
choices: It needs a tighter rank order so the ten priorities can compete more cleanly.
It needs a completion rule so older items leave before new items arrive.
It needs a posteriorities side so important work has room around it.
questions.explanation: A posteriorities list is as important as a priorities list. Ranking and completion rules still focus on doing; the key names what should stop, wait, move, or leave.
