questions.prompt: Kyle waits for better card-reader conditions while Hayes opens the cash box. Which response shows agency?
choices: Waiting fits because agency depends on conditions becoming easier first.
Opening the cash box fits because attention has returned to controllable behavior.
Both fit because agency is mostly the private feeling of staying hopeful.
questions.explanation: Agency grows when attention returns to controllable behavior. Waiting for ideal conditions can hide the move still within reach.

reviewCards.front: What is constructive self-talk in action?
reviewCards.back: It is inner language chosen on purpose to make the next responsible action easier. It names possibility, keeps the problem specific, asks for agency, and starts movement.

reviewCards.front: Why does an optimistic explanatory style keep a setback workable?
reviewCards.back: It treats the setback as temporary and specific instead of permanent and personal. The problem stays real, but it becomes small enough for a next action.

reviewCards.front: When does the "I can do it" cue actually help?
reviewCards.back: It helps when it interrupts hesitation and sends attention to the next move. If it only sounds pleasant and changes no behavior, it has become a slogan.

reviewCards.front: How does "what can I do now?" differ from a blame question?
reviewCards.back: It brings attention back to agency. A blame question may explain who was involved, but the responsibility question names the action still available now.

reviewCards.front: In one sentence, how does long-term consequence (Ch 4) connect to constructive self-talk?
reviewCards.back: Long-term consequence tells you which frog matters; constructive self-talk gives you the sentence that helps you start that frog before easier relief takes over.

reviewCards.front: What are the four parts of Action self-talk?
reviewCards.back: Name possibility, Keep it specific, Ask the agency question, and Start the next action. The last part keeps the tool tied to visible behavior.

implementationPlan.title: Say the Action Sentence
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice turning inner language into a start signal. Use Say the Action Sentence: name that the task is possible, make the problem specific, ask what you can do now, then begin the first visible move. The words count only if they change what your hands do next.

ifThenPlans.context: A setback starts to sound permanent or personal
ifThenPlans.plan: If your sentence uses always, never, or I am bad at this, then rewrite it as one specific, temporary problem you can touch.

ifThenPlans.context: You hesitate before the first visible move
ifThenPlans.plan: If you pause at the start, then say, "I can do it," and move one object tied to the task into working position.

ifThenPlans.context: A delay turns into complaint
ifThenPlans.plan: If your mind asks who made this happen, then ask what you can do now and write the smallest useful action.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before your next first work block, place the hardest task in plain sight. Rehearse once: say the action sentence, touch the file or tool, and make the first move.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Teach Say the Action Sentence to one person this week using a real stuck task. Have them test whether the sentence names a specific next action.

memorableLines.text: Mood can lag; motion can lead.
memorableLines.why: It captures why action can come before feeling ready.

memorableLines.text: A cue earns trust when it changes the next move.
memorableLines.why: It separates useful cue phrases from empty comfort.

memorableLines.text: Blame spends energy that responsibility can turn into work.
memorableLines.why: It makes the responsibility question memorable and practical.

chapters.title: Technology is a terrible master
chapters.hook: Your first 4 alerts can steal 40 minutes before the hard task has a name.
chapters.counterintuition: Technology is not the villain, but an unmanaged device will gladly become the boss. The laptop can draft the report or train your hand to chase every badge.
chapters.tryThisNow: Within 24 hours, the first time alerts pull you from hard work, schedule 15 minutes, rank 3 alerts by consequence, and mute 2.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Put technology under the work plan: rank incoming signals, schedule checking, disable weak alerts, and protect the block where the frog gets done.

breakdown.fastRead: Colby opens the report and sees four small badges bloom in the corner of the screen. Email, texts, app badges, and alerts all speak in the same urgent color, so his hand moves before his mind has chosen. A beep is not a boss. Technology boundaries mean you decide when messages get attention and when the frog gets the room. The first rule is simple: rank the signal before you obey it. If a tool cannot point to the day's real priority, it waits.
breakdown.deepRead:
A notification works by borrowing the costume of work. It arrives through the same machine that holds the report, the budget, and the client file. That makes the click feel responsible even when it is only checking.

Deborah keeps her status light green while she edits a proposal. Each incoming email feels small enough to answer. The cost hides in the restart. She has to find the paragraph again, rebuild the sentence in her head, and remember why the number on the page mattered. Interruptions do not cost only their seconds. They also take the trail you were following.

The loudest signal rarely deserves first place. A red badge may mean a true problem, a routine copy, or a message that can wait until the next check window. Treating all three as equal lets the device rank your day. The work plan should rank the device instead.

That is why a boundary has to be deliberate. Good intentions do not stop a busy message stream. A clear rule does. Disable alerts that do not change the next hour. Schedule message checking so you can answer well. Protect a focused block so the hard task gets more than scraps. Restore choice by making the tool serve the plan.
breakdown.fullRead:
Connor writes three items on a sticky note before he starts: finish the proposal, check client mail, review team chat. The proposal is the frog. The other two are real work, which is what makes them dangerous. If he treats every work app as harmless, the morning breaks into pieces before the proposal has a clean page.

A digital boundary is not a retreat from responsibility. It is a way to sort responsibility. Some messages matter now. Some matter later. Some only feel important because the device makes them bright. The useful move is not to hate technology. The useful move is to put each signal in its place.

Stella learns the hard version during an always-available week. Her manager expects fast replies. Her proposal needs quiet. If she stays visible all day, she earns a reputation for speed and loses the work that would prove judgment. If she disappears without notice, people may wait on her. She writes one line before the next block: "I am offline for proposal work and will check messages after this block." It costs her the comfort of seeming instantly useful.

That cost is real. Turning off alerts can make you feel absent. A calendar block can feel rude when other people are used to getting you on demand. A device fast can feel odd in the hand, like reaching for a cup that is not there. A boundary costs the comfort of instant reply. The trade is worth it only when the protected work matters more than the quick proof that you are available.

Coralie tests this with Kevin in a short call before a client deadline. Kevin says, "If I mute email, I may miss something." Coralie asks, "Which messages can change the proposal in the next hour?" Kevin names two senders. She says, "Then keep those, mute the rest, and set the check window." No speech about willpower is needed. The boundary follows the ranked risk.

Celine expects a one-hour digital fast to make her anxious. The reveal is stranger: after ten minutes, the room gets quieter. Her hand still reaches for the phone once, then twice, and finds nothing to do. That tiny reach teaches the rule better than a lecture. Much checking is automatic. When the device is off for a defined period, the habit shows itself.

The rule can be abused. A person can hide behind a boundary and ignore duties that need a timely answer. The rule is not "never check." It is "check on purpose." Use Disable alerts, Schedule checking, Protect focused work, and Restore choice as a four-part Technology boundary. If an alert has real consequence now, answer it. If it only proves you are reachable, let it wait while the frog gets done.

examples.title: Colby's Badge Mistake
examples.scenario: Colby is halfway through the first paragraph of the proposal when email, texts, app badges, and alerts stack in the screen corner. His hand opens the inbox before he has chosen to stop. The mistake lands in his stomach: the inbox is now setting the order. He closes it, writes "proposal first" on the pad, and keeps only the one client alert that can change the next hour.
examples.whatToDo: Colby names the interruption as his own slip, not the device's fault. He closes the inbox, ranks the alerts by consequence, and mutes the ones that cannot change the proposal block.
examples.whyItMatters: The useful moment is the noticing. Readers can recover from a bad click by ranking the signal and returning the device to servant status.

examples.title: Deborah's Green Light
examples.scenario: The green status dot beside Deborah's name looks helpful. I am being professional, she thinks. The solo work underneath the chat window waits. One reply will be quick. Then another arrives. The thought changes shape: if I am always available, other people's timing wins, and the proposal gets attention scraps. She changes the status to focusing and writes the next line before checking again.
examples.whatToDo: Deborah changes her status before the next reply tempts her. She gives the solo work a protected stretch and leaves message checking for the scheduled window.
examples.whyItMatters: Always available can feel like service while it hands the schedule to everyone else. The status change makes the boundary visible enough to keep.

examples.title: Connor's Device Fast Plan
examples.scenario: Before opening any app, Connor draws three boxes on a desk note: turn devices off, message check, frog. The phone can stay on and soothe him, or it can go dark for a defined period while the report begins. He has one hour of clean attention and knows automatic checking will tug at him. He assigns forty minutes to the frog, ten to checking, and ten to a buffer for real consequences.
examples.whatToDo: Connor plans the device fast before the work starts. He turns devices off for the focused period and leaves one scheduled check for messages that might truly matter.
examples.whyItMatters: The planning happens before the habit wakes up. A defined period makes the boundary specific enough to test, not merely admire.

examples.title: Stella's Availability Trade
examples.scenario: Stella's team channel fills while her solo work, a budget plan, sits unfinished. Always available feels safer than silence. She weighs two poor choices: answer every note and let other people's timing thin the plan, or vanish and leave two people waiting. She writes a narrow promise: proposal work now, message check after the block, urgent budget blockers only in the marked thread.
examples.whatToDo: Stella gives the team a boundary with a channel for true blockers. She protects the priority work without pretending other people have no needs.
examples.whyItMatters: Technology boundaries are not a license to disappear. They work best when the reader sorts real consequence from the pressure to seem reachable.

examples.title: Coralie and Kevin Rank
examples.scenario: "If I mute email, I may miss the client," Kevin says on the video call. Coralie asks, "Which alerts can change the draft in the next hour?" "The client, legal, and Connor." "Then keep those three," she says. "Mute app badges and team chatter until the check window." Kevin nods and changes the settings before reopening the draft.
examples.whatToDo: Kevin keeps the alerts tied to real consequence and mutes the rest. Coralie makes the ranking plain enough that he can act during the call.
examples.whyItMatters: A ranked alert list beats a vague promise to focus. The reader can see which signals serve the work and which signals only create noise.

examples.title: Celine's Quiet Hour
examples.scenario: Celine expects the instruction to turn devices off to feel like losing a tool. The phone is off for a defined period, the laptop alerts are off, and the sketch file is open. Ten minutes later, the surprise is not panic. It is her hand reaching toward the blank place beside the keyboard. The digital fast reveals automatic checking and the small dependency behind it.
examples.whatToDo: Celine leaves the devices off for the defined period and marks each automatic reach on a sticky note. She uses the count to choose which alert to disable next.
examples.whyItMatters: Temporary disconnection makes the invisible habit visible. Once the checking urge has a count, the reader can change a setting instead of trusting willpower.

questions.prompt: A work log shows Colby opened 8 alerts before writing one proposal sentence. Which reading best fits the source idea?
choices: The tools are shaping the workday because each alert breaks the task into fragments.
The tools are improving the workday because each alert might carry useful news.
The tools are recording the workday because each alert can be handled later.
questions.explanation: Unmanaged technology fragments attention. The near miss is assuming every alert makes work better because it arrives through a work tool.

questions.prompt: Two proposal writers see the same red email badge. One treats it as urgent; one asks what consequence changes now. Which response fits?
choices: The second response fits because notifications can create urgency before consequence exists.
The first response fits because notifications are neutral information until answered.
Both responses fit because every red badge deserves the same immediate check.
questions.explanation: Notifications create false urgency. Asking about consequence separates a real signal from a bright demand with no immediate cost.

questions.prompt: Deborah stays reachable all morning and finishes only scraps of solo work. What should she infer first?
choices: Her availability is proving professionalism because fast replies build trust.
Her availability may be letting other people's timing set the priority work.
Her availability should expand because solo work can fit around all messages.
questions.explanation: Constant availability can undermine priority work. It may look professional while it gives the best attention to other people's timing.

questions.prompt: Kevin opens messages before the budget frog, says the scan will clear his head, and still has no first sentence after 12 minutes. What should he call that pattern?
choices: Read it as preparation when the scan helps him settle before writing.
Read it as triage when the scan tells him which messages can wait.
Read it as avoidance when the scan replaces the first hard sentence.
questions.explanation: Checking can feel productive while avoiding the frog. The warmup story is tempting because it sounds like work.

questions.prompt: Connor says he has enough discipline to ignore his phone, but he keeps reaching for it. Which response fits the source idea?
choices: He should trust discipline because boundaries matter only after habits fail.
He should check more often because frequent checks reduce the urge to reach.
He should set a deliberate boundary because willpower alone is not the rule.
questions.explanation: A device boundary must be deliberate. Discipline can help, but the rule asks for a visible limit the next reach has to meet.

questions.prompt: A calendar block names the frog, but the inbox keeps rearranging the morning. What should lead?
choices: The work plan should lead, with technology checked inside chosen windows.
The inbox should lead, with the calendar adjusted around incoming messages.
The newest message should lead, with the frog resumed after each reply.
questions.explanation: Technology should be subordinate to the work plan. Incoming messages may matter, but they do not get automatic command.

questions.prompt: A log shows 6 tiny interruptions in one focus block, each under a minute. What should Stella count besides seconds?
choices: She should count only the seconds because short interruptions have short costs.
She should count the restart cost because each break steals the work trail.
She should count only the message count because recovery happens by itself.
questions.explanation: Interruptions carry recovery costs. The break also forces the worker to rebuild the sentence, problem, or decision.

questions.prompt: Coralie's work chat app carries client facts, legal notes, idle chatter, and app badges in the same stream. Which reading is strongest?
choices: The app should be treated as a work lane because client facts arrive there.
The app should be ranked carefully because work and distraction share one stream.
The app should be answered in order because mixed streams stay fair that way.
questions.explanation: Digital tools are most dangerous when they blend work and distraction. The work label can hide the need to rank the stream.

questions.prompt: Celine turns off noncritical alerts before a device-off work block, while leaving one urgent client channel open. How should the source idea judge that move?
choices: It protects coverage when she scans all alerts just before the block.
It protects response time when she leaves every channel open.
It protects focus when muted alerts cannot change the block.
questions.explanation: Turning off alerts can be a productivity act. The key condition is that the muted alerts do not carry real consequence for the block.

reviewCards.front: What are technology boundaries in plain work language?
reviewCards.back: They are rules that make messages, notifications, feeds, and devices serve chosen priorities. The tool can help, but it does not get to choose the next task.

reviewCards.front: Why can a notification stream feel more important than it is?
reviewCards.back: Email, texts, app badges, and alerts borrow the look of urgency. The reader has to rank consequence before treating the signal as command.

reviewCards.front: How does always available work steal attention without looking lazy?
reviewCards.back: It turns other people's timing into the default schedule. The worker stays busy and helpful while solo work gets attention scraps.

reviewCards.front: What does self-imposed urgency (Ch 13) get WRONG if you applied it naively to a technology-boundary case?
reviewCards.back: It can make every fast reply feel mature. With technology boundaries, urgency must be ranked by consequence, or self-pressure just becomes quicker obedience to the device.

reviewCards.front: What does a short digital fast reveal that ordinary focus advice can miss?
reviewCards.back: Turning devices off for a defined period exposes automatic checking. The reach for the absent phone shows which habit needs a setting change.

implementationPlan.title: Rank the Signal
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice making technology answer to the work plan. Use Rank the Signal: name the frog, list the incoming channels, then sort each signal by real consequence for the next block. The skill ends with one visible setting, status, or calendar choice.

ifThenPlans.context: A red badge makes a message feel urgent
ifThenPlans.plan: If a badge pulls your hand toward the inbox, then Rank the Signal by asking what consequence changes before the next check window.

ifThenPlans.context: Being always available starts to crowd out solo work
ifThenPlans.plan: If your status light is protecting everyone else's timing, then Rank the Signal and post the next check window before the focus block.

ifThenPlans.context: Turning off alerts feels irresponsible
ifThenPlans.plan: If muting alerts feels risky, then Rank the Signal and leave on only channels that can change the protected work block.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, the first time a notification interrupts a hard task, create a calendar block for the next open focus slot. Use Rank the Signal inside that block: list three active channels, rank them by consequence, mute the bottom two, and write the one task the block protects.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Use spaced reps three times this week. First, rank signals before one work block. Two days later, add a device-off period. At week's end, protect a longer block and keep only consequence-ranked alerts.

memorableLines.text: A beep is not a boss.
memorableLines.why: It turns the chapter's rule into a quick test.

memorableLines.text: The loudest signal rarely deserves first place.
memorableLines.why: It makes the ranking move easy to remember.

memorableLines.text: A boundary costs the comfort of instant reply.
memorableLines.why: It names the tradeoff without softening it.

chapters.title: Technology is a wonderful servant
chapters.hook: Is the device in your hand running your priorities, or running its own notifications?
chapters.counterintuition: Servant tools have teeth: the same screen can scatter a morning and protect the work that matters. The difference is the job you give it before it starts talking back.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before you send your next reply, spend 10 minutes reviewing one recent tool miss and write one line: This tool should serve ____ by ____.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Make each tool pass the servant test: Define objective, Choose tool, Reduce friction, and Measure output before novelty steals the work.

breakdown.fastRead:
William's calendar flashes while the hard proposal is still open. The alert is not there to make him feel busy. It guards a priority appointment, the block where the frog gets first claim on his mind. A reminder can either pull him toward noise or back to the work he chose.

Tools should earn their keep. Technology serves when it automates, organizes, teaches, reminds, or carries a message toward a chosen result. It fails when it becomes a second task made of settings and feeds. The Servant technology test is plain: Define objective, Choose tool, Reduce friction, Measure output. If the tool does not help the frog move, it is not serving yet.
breakdown.deepRead:
A tool becomes useful when it removes a small drag from important work. The drag might be memory, setup, weak skill, repeated typing, or a message that needs to be clear before it leaves the screen. A calendar can hold a priority appointment. An online course can close a skill gap. A template can spare the mind from rebuilding the same low-judgment step again.

Yann sees this at his course desk with an online course paused beside an unfinished report. He does not browse the course catalog for a pleasant lesson. He writes the gap first: weak chart labels slow every weekly report. Then he searches for the shortest lesson on clear chart titles and practices on the next graph. The course earns its place because it helps one real file improve.

Servant technology starts with control. Define objective means name the result before the tool chooses the room. Choose tool means pick the smallest device, app, course, template, alarm, or search that fits that result. Reduce friction means make the next good step easier to start. Measure output means check whether the work moved, not whether the tool felt new.

Novelty is not output. A shiny app can make the day feel modern while the frog still waits. A dull calendar block can be more valuable than a new dashboard if it protects the first hour of real work.
breakdown.fullRead:
Rachel's monthly report shipped early only after the team looked backward at the evidence. The finished file had fewer copy errors, fewer late replies, and no missing chart labels. The cause was not a burst of willpower. Two weeks earlier, Rachel had turned the repeated header, chart note, and closing paragraph into a template. The keyboard shortcut did not do the thinking. It kept the low-judgment setup from eating the thinking.

That is the best place for automation: repeated steps that waste attention but do not need fresh judgment. A template can hold the report frame. A shortcut can paste the same meeting link. A calendar reminder can guard the priority appointment. These tools are not the frog. They clear the mud around the frog.

The danger is making the tool the hero. Nancy catches herself halfway through a settings tour for a new task app. The proposal file is closed. The app has eight color choices open. She notices the swap: she has traded the high-value task for a neat control panel. She closes the settings, opens the proposal, and writes the first rough paragraph. Let the task choose the tool.

Communication needs the same rule. Hailey's draft reply has three links, two updates, and one vague request. Before sending, she writes a line above the draft: "Purpose: get one approval by Friday." That line cuts the reply in half. More messages would not help. A purposeful message has a job. It should make the next action easier for the person reading it.

The Servant technology test keeps the order straight. Define objective before picking the app. Choose tool after the result is clear. Reduce friction by removing a repeat step, a memory load, or a skill gap. Measure output by checking the visible work: the protected appointment happened, the chart improved, the report shipped, the reply got a clear answer.

Bryce and Brandon show the split. Bryce opens every new writing tool his feed recommends and ends the day with a tidy setup but no draft. Brandon keeps one plain template for recurring proposals, one calendar block for the first draft, and one search note for the skill he is missing. Bryce has more tools. Brandon has more output.

Do the opposite when the work needs human judgment, care, or direct talk. Do not automate a hard apology, a sensitive choice, or a question that needs a real conversation. In those moments, the servant tool may be a blank page that helps you write one honest sentence before you speak. The screen is useful only while it stays under the work.

examples.title: William's Calendar Restart
examples.scenario: William's cursor is already inside a message reply when the Calendar and reminder system slides a priority appointment onto his lock screen. He stops before typing the first word. The old routine would clear messages until the proposal felt too late. He closes the inbox, opens the proposal file, and restarts the morning with the calendar guarding the frog.
examples.whatToDo: William treats the calendar alert as a command to protect the priority appointment. He closes the reply and opens the hard file before the message thread can set the hour.
examples.whyItMatters: The pause shows the servant rule in motion. A reminder helps only when it sends attention back to the chosen objective instead of adding one more signal.

examples.title: Yann's Course Notebook
examples.scenario: Yann's course desk holds a laptop, a chipped mug, and one page labeled "chart titles." The Online learning tool is paused at minute six. He skips broad online courses and audio programs, uses search tools for short labels, and returns to the report. No grand plan appears. The lesson meets one performance gap.
examples.whatToDo: Yann names the exact skill gap before learning. He watches only the lesson that helps the next chart title and applies it to the report in front of him.
examples.whyItMatters: The detail keeps online learning from becoming browsing. A course serves when it builds a skill needed for execution, not when it fills a quiet hour.

examples.title: Rachel's Template Evidence
examples.scenario: Rachel's monthly report is already sent when the review begins. The evidence sits in the change log: fewer copied headers, one keyboard shortcut for the standard note, and a Template and automation file for the recurring work. The cleaner result came from removing repeated setup, not from asking the team to think less.
examples.whatToDo: Rachel keeps the template for repeatable parts and leaves the analysis open for judgment. She uses the shortcut only where the step is low-judgment and repeated.
examples.whyItMatters: The postmortem marks the right target for automation. Repetition can be trimmed so attention is saved for the work that still needs thought.

examples.title: Nancy Catches the Settings Swap
examples.scenario: Nancy has the proposal closed and the task app open to color settings. The mistake lands when she sees the blank document behind the window. Purposeful tool use was supposed to support the high-value task, yet the tool has become the task. She closes the settings panel and writes the first rough paragraph.
examples.whatToDo: Nancy names the swap out loud: the tool is not the output. She reopens the proposal and uses the app only to hold the next work block.
examples.whyItMatters: The noticing matters more than the fix. A reader can catch the moment a tool starts asking for service and put the objective back in charge.

examples.title: Hailey's Reply Memo
examples.scenario: Hailey's unsent reply sits beside a calendar block labeled "highest-value task." Her small memo uses the Servant technology test: "Objective: get one approval by Friday. Tool: short email. Output: yes, no, or missing condition." The draft below it shrinks from five paragraphs to six clear lines. The technology can carry the message, but the memo gives it a job.
examples.whatToDo: Hailey writes the objective line before sending. She cuts any link, aside, or update that does not help the reader give the needed approval.
examples.whyItMatters: The memo turns communication into servant technology. A message serves when it moves one clear response, not when it proves the sender worked hard.

examples.title: Bryce and Brandon Split
examples.scenario: By Friday, Bryce has tried three writing apps, a fresh dashboard, and a new automation menu. His proposal has a title and little else. Brandon works from the Servant technology test: Define objective, Choose tool, Reduce friction, Measure output. He keeps one template, one calendar block, and one finished draft.
examples.whatToDo: Bryce chases the tool stack, while Brandon lets the objective choose the tool. Brandon measures the draft produced, not the number of features explored.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast makes the output test plain. A tool is valuable only when it reduces friction around important work and leaves visible progress behind.

questions.prompt: William has three new work apps open before naming the result he wants. Which first move fits purposeful tool use?
choices: He should test the newest app first and keep whichever feels fastest.
He should name the objective first, then choose the tool that serves it.
He should keep all three apps open so no possible feature is lost.
questions.explanation: Technology should serve a chosen objective. Starting with the app treats novelty as progress before the result has a job for the tool.

questions.prompt: A calendar log shows Nancy missed two proposal blocks after meetings ran long. What should she infer from the pattern?
choices: The calendar mainly stored meeting times and did not need to protect work blocks.
The calendar should guard priority appointments, not just record other people's meetings.
The calendar worked well if it kept a full record of every meeting.
questions.explanation: Digital tools can protect priority appointments. Treating the calendar as storage misses its job of defending the chosen work block.

questions.prompt: Yann wants to improve a report and has a search tab full of online courses. Which choice best uses the learning tool?
choices: He should browse several popular courses before naming the report skill.
He should save a broad course list so future gaps feel covered.
He should pick the lesson tied to the report skill that is slowing him.
questions.explanation: Online learning helps when it meets a real performance gap. A broad course list can feel useful while the weak report skill stays untouched.

questions.prompt: Rachel's team wants to automate a recurring report. Which boundary should guide the choice?
choices: They should automate the parts that require the freshest judgment first.
They should automate every step the software can reach during report week.
They should automate repeated low-judgment steps and keep analysis human.
questions.explanation: Automation belongs on repeated low-judgment steps. Applying it everywhere can remove attention from places that still need judgment.

questions.prompt: Hailey compares two tools for the same reply: one removes setup friction, the other adds features. Which test matters most?
choices: Choose the tool that makes the important reply easier to finish.
Choose the tool with the richer feature set for later possibilities.
Choose the tool that makes the task feel more impressive to manage.
questions.explanation: The right tool reduces friction around important work. Features are a near miss when they draw attention away from finishing the reply.

questions.prompt: Bryce ends Friday with a new dashboard and no draft. Brandon ends with an old template and a finished proposal. Which reading fits the output test?
choices: Brandon used the stronger tool because output, not novelty, proved its value.
Bryce used the stronger tool because newer software showed more range.
Both used strong tools if each setup felt organized by Friday.
questions.explanation: A tool should be judged by output. A new dashboard can feel useful, but the finished proposal is the better proof.

questions.prompt: A reminder pops up for Rachel, but the task name is vague. What should happen before she trusts the alert?
choices: She should add more reminders so one of them catches the right task.
She should follow the alert because any reminder creates priority.
She should clarify the priority the reminder is meant to support.
questions.explanation: Reminders support commitments when priorities are clear. More alerts cannot solve the problem of an unclear task.

questions.prompt: Nancy drafts a reply with five updates, but she needs one approval. Which revision makes communication serve the work?
choices: Cut the reply to the request that helps the reader approve, decline, or name the missing condition.
Add the extra updates so the reader sees the full work behind the request.
Send separate messages for each update so communication stays visible.
questions.explanation: Purposeful communication makes the next action easier. More updates can bury the approval the work actually needs.

questions.prompt: A powerful app starts suggesting new flows before Brandon has named the proposal result. Which response keeps user control?
choices: He should accept the app's flow so the stronger software can guide the work.
He should state the result first and use only the flow that serves it.
He should explore the suggested flows until the best one feels clear.
questions.explanation: Servant technology requires user control. The app can help only after Brandon names the result it must serve.

reviewCards.front: What are the four parts of the Servant technology test?
reviewCards.back: Define objective, Choose tool, Reduce friction, and Measure output. The order keeps the task in charge before the device, app, course, or template starts shaping the work.

reviewCards.front: How does a calendar become servant technology instead of storage?
reviewCards.back: It protects a priority appointment with the high-value task. The calendar is not just a record of meetings; it sends attention back to the work already chosen.

reviewCards.front: Recall long-term consequence (Ch 4): name one concrete moment here where it actually bites.
reviewCards.back: Bryce and Brandon make the consequence visible: Bryce collects tools, while Brandon finishes a proposal. The later result proves the plain template mattered more than the new dashboard.

reviewCards.front: Why should online courses, audio programs, or search tools start with a performance gap?
reviewCards.back: Online courses, audio programs, and search tools serve only when they build the skill needed for execution. Without a performance gap, learning can become comfortable delay.

reviewCards.front: Where does automation belong in recurring work?
reviewCards.back: Use it on repeated low-judgment steps: copied headers, standard notes, routine links, and other setup drag. Keep judgment, analysis, and sensitive choices in human hands.

reviewCards.front: What warning sign shows a tool has stopped serving?
reviewCards.back: The tool starts asking for attention while the frog stays untouched. Settings, feeds, features, or dashboards become the work instead of helping the work move.

implementationPlan.title: Run the Servant Tool Test
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice making a tool prove its service before it earns your time. Name the objective, choose the smallest fitting tool, remove one friction point, and check the output. The skill is not using more technology; it is keeping technology under the frog.

ifThenPlans.context: If a new app looks tempting before the task is named
ifThenPlans.plan: If a new app pulls your attention, then run the Servant Tool Test on paper. Write the objective first and open the app only if it reduces a real friction point.

ifThenPlans.context: If a recurring task starts with the same setup again
ifThenPlans.plan: If the setup is repeated and low-judgment, then make one template or shortcut. Use it to protect attention for the part that needs thought.

ifThenPlans.context: If a reminder fires and the task still feels vague
ifThenPlans.plan: If the alert names no clear priority, then rewrite the calendar block with the actual frog. Let the reminder guard a commitment, not a blur.

ifThenPlans.context: If a reply grows longer while the needed response stays unclear
ifThenPlans.plan: If the draft keeps expanding, then write one objective line above it. Cut the message until it asks for the response the work needs.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next 24 hours, before one work reply, write one line above the draft: This tool should serve ____ by ____. Send only after the line has changed the message.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For seven days, keep a daily log with four columns: tool used, frog served, friction removed, output seen. At week's end, drop one tool that filled a column with no output.

memorableLines.text: Tools should earn their keep.
memorableLines.why: It turns the servant standard into a sentence the reader can use before opening an app.

memorableLines.text: Novelty is not output.
memorableLines.why: It cuts through the common mistake of treating a new tool as proof of progress.

memorableLines.text: Let the task choose the tool.
memorableLines.why: It gives the reader a short rule for keeping technology under the work.

chapters.title: Focus your attention
chapters.hook: I used to call every fast reply responsible; could the open thread be the leak in your best hour?
chapters.counterintuition: What looks like staying available is often giving your best task a broken mind. Attention protection works when the screen, message threads, and quiet interval all point at one chosen task.
chapters.tryThisNow: The next time you feel the pull to check messages, close every extra window, leave one task visible, and say, "What answer can wait until this quiet interval ends?"
chapters.keyTakeaway: Protect attention before resistance starts: choose one task, remove competing inputs, work without interruption, and return to the next action when your mind slips.

breakdown.fastRead:
Janet watches a learner lose the task without leaving the training room. One spreadsheet is open, then a chat pane flashes, then a second document appears. The learner says she is still working, but her eyes have already split the job into pieces.

Focus means aiming your mind at one chosen task and guarding it from rival inputs. A priority without protected attention is only a named wish. Close the extra windows. Let one screen show the document, call plan, or spreadsheet that matters now. When a message thread pulls at you, name the pull and come back to the current line.
breakdown.deepRead:
Hazel sees Chantal's cursor stall after a client thread closes. Part of Chantal's mind is still with the last message, the half-read reply, and the question it wants to answer. That leftover pull is attention residue: a bit of yesterday's screen clinging to the task in front of you.

Hazel hears it in Chantal's voice during a project call. Chantal says, "I answered the client, then came right back." Hazel asks, "Did your mind come back with you?" The shared document is open, but Chantal keeps rereading the same line. The message thread is closed; the worry from the thread is not.

This is why focus needs design before you feel strong or weak. First choose the task. Then remove inputs: close tabs, mute the thread, clear the second document, and leave the selected priority visible. Next, give the work an uninterrupted stretch. Last, when your mind runs off, point it at one visible action instead of judging yourself.

Every open thread asks your task to start over. The cost is not only the seconds spent clicking. The cost is the shallow return. You reenter the hard task with part of your mind still composing, defending, or checking. A quiet interval gives the work enough continuity for structure, insight, or completion to appear.
breakdown.fullRead:
Presley learns the focus rule twice on the same screen. In the first pass, the proposal file shares space with a message thread, a calendar box, and three tabs from yesterday. He writes four careful lines, answers one ping, returns, and reads the four lines again as if someone else wrote them.

Later the screen is plain. One document fills it. No thread is visible. The notes for the proposal sit beside the keyboard, and the next section title is visible at the top of the page. Presley still has to think. The task has not become easy. But the screen no longer argues with him about what deserves the next glance.

This is the practical edge of attention protection. It is not a slogan about being intense. It is a setup that changes behavior before the drift begins. Choose task. Remove inputs. Work uninterrupted. Return when distracted. Those four moves are simple enough to repeat and strict enough to matter.

Responsiveness is the trap that makes the rule feel rude. Tobias can almost hear the message thread while he drafts the budget note. Someone may need him. The reply may be quick. It may even feel kind to answer now. Then he notices the budget sentence has not changed in five minutes. He says nothing to the room because he is alone, but the thought lands: quick replies can steal slow work.

The answer is not to become unreachable forever. The answer is to protect the interval that lets the frog move. A no-interruption interval can be short, but it has to be real. During it, the chosen task gets the whole screen, the whole next action, and the first claim on your attention. Quiet is a work tool, not a mood.

Cyrus plans his afternoon before any action begins. He has one hard task, one client thread, one spreadsheet, and enough nervous energy to touch all three. He writes the focus interval on a card: choose task, remove inputs, work uninterrupted, return when distracted. The card does not do the work. It keeps his scarce attention from being spent by accident.

Lawrence faces the harder version. A manager wants a fast answer in a message thread while the draft due today still has a blank middle. If he answers now, the draft loses its best hour. If he waits, the manager may wonder why he has gone quiet. Lawrence sends one plain line: "I am in a quiet interval on the draft and will answer when it ends." Then he closes the thread and writes the next paragraph.

Attention protection misleads the person whose job is live response itself: an emergency dispatcher, front-desk triage lead, or on-call support owner. For that role, the incoming signal is the task. For everyone else, the test is visible output. If the priority does not get protected attention, it remains a label while the day gets spent somewhere else.

examples.title: Janet's One-Screen Drill
examples.scenario: In the training room, Janet asks a new analyst to finish one document on one screen. The learner leaves a chat pane, an old spreadsheet, and the selected priority visible together. "I am watching all of it," she says. Janet does not scold. She asks the class to name which window the next sentence belongs to, and the confusion becomes the lesson.
examples.whatToDo: Janet has the learner close the extra tabs and keep only the document that matches the selected priority on the screen.
examples.whyItMatters: The drill makes focus visible. When the screen shows one task, the learner gets fewer invitations to drift before the work has depth.

examples.title: Presley's Plain Screen
examples.scenario: Presley's proposal opens first beside a message thread, a calendar box, and three tabs from yesterday. He writes four lines and rereads them twice after each ping. Later, the same document fills one screen. Closed tabs leave only the selected priority and a note page. The work is still hard, but his next sentence no longer has to compete for the screen.
examples.whatToDo: Presley changes the visible field before he keeps writing. He closes the extra windows and lets the proposal document own the screen.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast shows that environment can protect attention before willpower is tested. The same writer works better when the screen stops arguing with the task.

examples.title: Hazel Checks the Return
examples.scenario: During Tuesday's shared document call, Hazel listens as Chantal says, "I answered two message threads and came back." Chantal is the project lead. Hazel asks, "Did your mind come back too?" Chantal laughs, then reads the same hard task line for the third time. "The threads are closed," she says. Hazel replies, "The attention residue is not."
examples.whatToDo: Hazel has Chantal say the next sentence before touching the thread again. Chantal returns to the hard task by naming the next action.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange separates closing a message from recovering depth. Attention residue costs more than a few seconds when the mind keeps drafting the reply.

examples.title: Tobias Names the Next Line
examples.scenario: In Friday's budget draft, Tobias sits as the finance lead with one blank line under "cash risk." The client thread tugs at him. Maybe the reply is quick. Maybe silence looks careless. Maybe the budget is the wrong task. He catches the last thought before it hardens. The task is not wrong; his attention is loose. One number first, then the sentence.
examples.whatToDo: Tobias returns to the next visible action. He writes the number the budget note needs before he lets the message thread back into view.
examples.whyItMatters: Internal distraction does not need a speech or a diagnosis. The useful move is returning attention to the next action the chosen task requires.

examples.title: Cyrus Plans the Interval
examples.scenario: Before he opens anything, Cyrus writes three claims on an afternoon card: one client thread, one spreadsheet, one hard task. He has forty useful minutes of attention, not enough for all three at once. Under Focus interval, he copies the order: Choose task, Remove inputs, Work uninterrupted, Return when distracted. The card spends the attention before the inbox can.
examples.whatToDo: Cyrus gives the hard task the first interval and writes which inputs will be removed before the screen opens.
examples.whyItMatters: Planning comes before resistance. The Focus interval turns scarce attention into a choice the reader can see before messages begin bidding for it.

examples.title: Lawrence's Quiet Reply
examples.scenario: Lawrence has an unsent email draft due today and a manager's message waiting in the thread. Replying now protects responsiveness but breaks the no-interruption interval. Waiting protects completion but may look careless. He writes one line in the thread, "I am in a quiet interval on the draft and will answer when it ends," then closes it.
examples.whatToDo: Lawrence gives a brief boundary, closes the message thread, and keeps the draft as the only visible task until the interval ends.
examples.whyItMatters: The scene shows the conflict honestly. Responsiveness can serve the work, but it can also break the continuity a hard task needs.

questions.prompt: Two analysts start the same report. One leaves every chat open; one protects one report window. Which start best protects attention?
choices: The open-chat start keeps enough context to work without delay.
The mixed-window start proves the analyst can handle several inputs.
The one-report start treats attention as limited and worth guarding.
questions.explanation: Attention is limited, so the protected report window fits the lesson. The other starts assume attention can divide without meaningful loss.

questions.prompt: A work log shows six message checks during one hard task, with the same paragraph reread after each check. What should Presley infer?
choices: The checks are reducing depth because each return has a mental cost.
The checks are harmless because each one takes only a few seconds.
The checks are useful because rereading keeps the paragraph fresh.
questions.explanation: Task switching reduces depth. The repeated rereading shows the cost is not just seconds; part of the mind is still in the thread.

questions.prompt: A screen has the draft, a chat pane, and yesterday's spreadsheet visible. Which reading best fits visible distraction?
choices: The extra panes preserve useful options as long as the draft stays open.
The extra panes invite drift even when the writer plans to ignore them.
The extra panes matter only after the writer actually clicks them.
questions.explanation: Visible distractions invite drift before a click happens. The near miss is thinking ignored panes are harmless just because the draft remains open.

questions.prompt: Chantal gets ten tiny fragments for a difficult outline and no quiet stretch. What should she protect first?
choices: She needs an uninterrupted interval long enough for structure to form.
She can get the same depth if each fragment is used with strong intent.
She should treat fragments as equal to a longer block when effort is high.
questions.explanation: A hard task needs duration, not only intent. Tiny fragments can help simple chores, but they rarely give a hard outline enough continuity.

questions.prompt: Before opening the afternoon report, Cyrus waits to feel focused before closing messages. Which revision fits the focus rule?
choices: He should treat focus as a trait and avoid changing the setup.
He should design the screen and inputs before resistance begins.
He should keep the setup open so he can prove discipline later.
questions.explanation: Focus should be designed before resistance starts. Waiting for a focused mood gives every input a chance to claim attention first.

questions.prompt: Lawrence can answer a manager instantly or keep the draft moving through its quiet interval. What conflict is he seeing?
choices: Fast responsiveness can compete with finishing the important task.
Fast responsiveness keeps the draft stronger by holding the manager close.
Fast responsiveness matters only when no important task exists.
questions.explanation: Responsiveness can conflict with completion. The instant answer may feel responsible while breaking the continuity the draft needs.

questions.prompt: In a budget draft, Tobias feels a message tug while the risk line is blank. Which response matches internal distraction?
choices: He should treat the tug as proof that the budget is the wrong task.
He should return to the next budget action before judging the task.
He should open the thread briefly so the tug stops asking for attention.
questions.explanation: Internal distraction is handled by returning to the next action. The tug is not proof the task is wrong, and opening the thread feeds the switch.

questions.prompt: One workstation shows only the call plan. Another shows the call plan, inbox, and two open reports. Which setup best supports focus?
choices: The crowded setup supports focus because more context is ready.
The mixed setup supports focus because intention matters more than place.
The single-task setup supports focus because the environment matches the task.
questions.explanation: Focus improves when the environment matches the task. The crowded setup gives attention extra targets, even if the worker means well.

questions.prompt: Presley ranked the proposal first on Monday, then gave it six scraps of time between message checks. What is missing from his plan?
choices: A clearer priority label that proves the proposal is important.
A stronger memory of why the proposal was chosen first.
Protected attention that turns the chosen priority into output.
questions.explanation: Attention turns priority into finished output. A label or memory can name importance, but the proposal still needs protected work time.

reviewCards.front: What does attention protection mean in plain words?
reviewCards.back: It means choosing one important task, removing rival inputs, giving the task an uninterrupted stretch, and returning to the next action when the mind wanders.

reviewCards.front: Why does the one-screen task help a hard priority?
reviewCards.back: One screen makes the selected priority the only visible claim. Closed tabs and hidden threads make the next sentence easier to find than the next distraction.

reviewCards.front: How does attention residue make a quick message cost more than seconds?
reviewCards.back: Part of the mind keeps drafting, defending, or checking the message after the thread closes. The return to the hard task is shallower than it looks.

reviewCards.front: What does a quiet interval give a hard task that fragments cannot?
reviewCards.back: It gives continuity. With no interruption, the task has enough time for structure, insight, or completion to build before the next input breaks the line of thought.

reviewCards.front: Name the four moves in a Focus interval.
reviewCards.back: Choose task, Remove inputs, Work uninterrupted, and Return when distracted. The order matters because setup protects attention before resistance starts.

reviewCards.front: Which matters more in a broken focus interval - frictionless start (Ch 9) or attention protection - and why?
reviewCards.back: In a broken interval, attention protection matters more. Frictionless start gets the task open, but rival inputs split the work before depth can build, so the interval must be guarded after the first move.

implementationPlan.title: Guard the Focus Interval
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice guarding one chosen task long enough for real progress to appear. Guard the Focus Interval by choosing the task, removing inputs, working without interruption, and returning to the next action when your mind wanders. The skill is not heroic willpower; it is designing fewer exits.

ifThenPlans.context: Your screen shows more than the chosen task
ifThenPlans.plan: If extra panes are visible, then close or hide them until one document, spreadsheet, or call plan fills the screen.

ifThenPlans.context: A message thread pulls you away mid-task
ifThenPlans.plan: If a thread pulls you away, then name the next action in the hard task before you decide whether to answer.

ifThenPlans.context: A hard task keeps breaking into fragments
ifThenPlans.plan: If a hard task is getting only scraps, then protect one no-interruption interval and define what completion looks like for that stretch.

ifThenPlans.context: Your mind wanders while the task is open
ifThenPlans.plan: If your mind wanders, then point to the next visible action and do that before judging the whole task.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: The next time you feel the pull to check a message thread, close every extra window and say aloud, "What answer can wait until this quiet interval ends?" Then do one next action.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, stage one real focus interval with another person aware of it. Ask one question before you begin, listen to the answer, then protect the interval as agreed.

memorableLines.text: A priority without protected attention is only a named wish.
memorableLines.why: It separates naming a priority from giving it the attention that finishes work.

memorableLines.text: Every open thread asks your task to start over.
memorableLines.why: It makes attention residue easy to remember and notice.

memorableLines.text: Quiet is a work tool, not a mood.
memorableLines.why: It turns quiet intervals into a practical work condition.

chapters.title: Slice and dice the task
chapters.hook: A job too big to face gets its first edge the moment you carve one thin slice off it.
chapters.counterintuition: A task can feel too large to hold in your head and still be small enough to touch with one slice. Size blocks the mood, not the next move.
chapters.tryThisNow: At your next handoff between tasks, move one sticky note onto a large task. Compare two first slices, choose the one tied to the result, and start it.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Big tasks shrink when you cut one visible slice, start it, and keep that slice tied to the result you still owe.

breakdown.fastRead:
Beatrice carries a sticky note from the edge of her folder to the blank pricing page. "The proposal is still huge," she tells Aline. "Good," Aline says. "Do not lift the whole thing. Punch one hole. Price one line."

Slice and dice means cut a large task into pieces small enough to start now. The Swiss cheese method makes small holes wherever the work can be entered. The salami slice method finishes one thin piece, then the next. A five-minute start gets the file open before the whole job feels possible. Small starts make big work touchable.
breakdown.deepRead:
A large task scares the mind by arriving all at once. The proposal, report, or tax file looks like one wall. A slice gives the wall an edge. Beatrice can see a pricing line. Pauline can see one receipt. Claire can see one source title.

At the receipt counter, Pauline keeps wiping the same clear patch beside a pile of receipts. "I am getting ready," she says. Aline moves one receipt beside the laptop. "No more ready. Five minutes, one receipt." Pauline types the coffee receipt and reaches for the next one before the mug cools.

That is why a small start works. It separates beginning from finishing. The job may still be large, but the body is now in contact with it. Momentum often comes after the first mark, not before it.

Swiss cheese holes fit tasks with many entry points. Write one paragraph, make one call, sort one pile, or list three missing facts. Salami slices fit tasks that need order. Finish the title slide, then the chart note, then the closing ask. One finished slice beats six open tabs.

Small does not mean loose. A useful slice can be seen and checked. "Improve the report" is fog. "Draft the first paragraph" is a slice.
breakdown.fullRead:
A finished job still matters. Slicing does not make a weak result acceptable. It only makes the first move small enough to take. Oscar can cut the memo into pieces, but the client still needs the recommendation.

On a client call, Oscar says, "I made six little slices." Aline asks, "Which one moves the memo?" Oscar reads the list: format headers, rename files, clean chart colors. Then he stops. "None of them says what we recommend." Aline says, "Then the next slice is the recommendation paragraph. Not the colors."

That is the hard part of slicing. Small pieces can become a neat hiding place. A person can feel busy while the frog stays untouched. The test is simple: does this slice move the larger outcome? If not, it is only motion.

Use three cuts. First, make Swiss cheese holes when the task has many good doors. Beatrice can price one line before she knows every paragraph. Claire can copy one source title before the whole report has shape. Each hole weakens the solid look of the task.

Second, use salami slices when order matters. Emmett handles a deck by finishing the first slide, then the next note, then the final ask. The slice is thin, but it is complete. That matters because completion gives the mind proof it can continue.

Third, use the five-minute start when resistance is the main barrier. Pauline does not promise to finish the tax file beside her laptop. She only opens it and enters one receipt. Once the file is open, the second receipt is easier to touch.

The method fails when the slice is not tied to behavior. A label on a note is not a cut. Beatrice has to write the number. Emmett has to complete one part. Pauline has to get the task open. Without a visible act, the method becomes another pleasant name for delay.

Pick a slice that is easy to identify. If the first step needs a speech, it is too cloudy. Say it in plain words: open the file, list the missing names, draft the first sentence, send the question, sort the first pile. Clear slices beat brave speeches.

Keep the big result on the page while the slice stays small. Put the final outcome at the top. Put the next slice under it. That stops small work from drifting into safe chores.

The counter-case is real. If Nash has a clean handoff note due before the meeting ends, slicing the heading again would waste the moment. He should send the good enough note. Slice the task to start the frog, not to keep it on the plate.

examples.title: Beatrice Prices One Line
examples.scenario: Everyone at the pricing review board expects Beatrice to ask for another day. The large task has blank sections, red comments, and a pricing page no one has touched. "So I need the whole draft before I can move?" she asks. Aline slides a sticky note onto one pricing line. "No. Make one Swiss cheese hole, a partial start." Ten minutes later, that line has a rough number.
examples.whatToDo: Beatrice moves the sticky note to one pricing line, writes the rough number, and leaves the rest of the proposal closed for the moment.
examples.whyItMatters: The Swiss cheese hole gives the task a point of entry. A partial start beats waiting for courage to cover the whole proposal.

examples.title: Emmett's Deck Thread
examples.scenario: Emmett types in the team thread: "Deck still feels huge." Aline answers, "Name the first salami slice, a thin slice." Emmett sends, "Title slide." Aline writes, "Complete one part. Then the chart note." Emmett asks, "Only those two?" Aline replies, "Yes. One finished slice beats six open tabs."
examples.whatToDo: Emmett finishes the title slide, then writes the chart note before opening the rest of the deck.
examples.whyItMatters: The salami slice method protects order. One completed piece builds motion without asking the reader to feel ready for the whole deck.

examples.title: Pauline Enters One Receipt
examples.scenario: The kettle clicks off while Pauline keeps wiping the clean side of the receipt counter. The tax receipts sit beside the laptop. "I am preparing again," she says. Aline puts one receipt on the keyboard. "Reset smaller. Five minutes is the initial interval. Get the task open." Pauline leaves the cloth in the sink and enters the coffee receipt.
examples.whatToDo: Pauline stops cleaning, moves one receipt onto the keyboard, and uses the five-minute start to enter that first item.
examples.whyItMatters: The five-minute start separates beginning from finishing. The reader can open the task before the whole file feels possible.

examples.title: Claire Copies the Source
examples.scenario: At the library table, Claire's large task has a heading and a wide blank middle. A pencil rests across the margin. Aline reads the heading aloud: "Evidence list." Claire copies one source title under it. The page still looks unfinished, but the Swiss cheese method has made one of the small holes that partial starts depend on.
examples.whatToDo: Claire writes one source title under the evidence heading and marks the next empty line for the following source.
examples.whyItMatters: A small hole makes avoidance less believable. The reader can enter a large task through any useful spot.

examples.title: Oscar Keeps the Memo Honest
examples.scenario: "I made six tiny slices," Oscar says on the client call. "Which salami slice is the thin slice that moves the memo?" Aline asks. Oscar checks the page. "The recommendation paragraph." "Then complete one part first." "Not the color pass?" "Only if color sends the memo." Oscar crosses out the polish task.
examples.whatToDo: Oscar chooses the recommendation paragraph as the next salami slice and drops the polish task until the memo has its main point.
examples.whyItMatters: Small pieces need a line back to the final result. Slicing should start the frog, not turn harmless chores into progress.

examples.title: Nash Catches the Setup
examples.scenario: Nash is labeling folders after the meeting when he notices the trick. The handoff note is blank, and the neat labels are cover. "Five minutes is the initial interval only if I get the task open," he tells Aline at the meeting-room doorway. He moves the folder under his pen and writes the first sentence. Continuing can wait until the real work has begun.
examples.whatToDo: Nash stops labeling folders, moves the handoff folder under his pen, and spends the five-minute start on the first sentence.
examples.whyItMatters: Momentum often appears after contact with the task. The short start must touch the real work, not the setup around it.

questions.prompt: Beatrice's proposal log shows three days of message cleanup and no movement on the proposal. Which first move fits slice and dice?
choices: She should wait for enough time to finish the proposal.
She should keep clearing light work until the proposal feels smaller.
She should divide the proposal and start one small piece.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 says large tasks should be divided into small pieces. The waiting choice treats size as a reason not to touch the proposal.

questions.prompt: Two people face the same heavy report: one waits to feel ready, and one drafts one rough paragraph. Which response fits?
choices: Waiting fits when the report deserves a calm full start.
Drafting fits because a small start can cut through resistance.
Waiting fits if easier work rebuilds confidence first.
questions.explanation: Fact 2 supports the small start. Waiting for the feeling to change keeps the report untouched.

questions.prompt: Claire's report now has one copied source title under a rough heading, with many blanks left. How should that partial work be read?
choices: It has made the report messier and less useful.
It should be replaced once the full outline is clear.
It has weakened avoidance by opening the task.
questions.explanation: Fact 3 says the Swiss cheese method uses partial work to weaken avoidance. The blanks can look messy, but the task has been entered.

questions.prompt: Emmett's deck has a title slide, a chart note, and a closing ask left before a deadline. Which move matches the salami slice method?
choices: Finish the first small section, then move to the next one.
Open every section so the whole deck feels active.
Wait for a longer work block because thin slices are too slow.
questions.explanation: Fact 4 says salami slices use sequential small completion. Opening everything can look active while no slice gets finished.

questions.prompt: Pauline says five minutes on the tax file is fake work because the file will remain unfinished. Which answer fits the source fact?
choices: The short start matters only if the tax file is completed.
The short start works after the task already feels easy.
The short start counts because beginning and finishing are separate.
questions.explanation: Fact 5 says a timed start separates beginning from finishing. Calling it fake work misses the value of getting the task open.

questions.prompt: Nash writes one handoff sentence after moving the folder under his pen, then keeps going for several more lines. What does that pattern show?
choices: Momentum should have appeared before the first sentence.
Momentum often appears after contact with the task.
Momentum proves the handoff note was not the real frog.
questions.explanation: Fact 6 says momentum often appears after contact. The near miss is waiting for momentum before the first sentence.

questions.prompt: Oscar writes two possible first slices for a memo: "improve the memo" and "draft the recommendation paragraph." Which one fits better?
choices: Improve the memo fits because broad wording leaves more room to adjust.
Draft the recommendation paragraph fits because the first slice is easy to identify.
Improve the memo fits if the details can be chosen while working.
questions.explanation: Fact 7 says the first slice should be easy to identify. Broad wording can hide the next move even when it sounds responsible.

questions.prompt: Aline sees a proposal broken into font checks and file names while the client recommendation stays blank. Which warning applies?
choices: Slicing should not become an excuse to avoid the whole result.
Slicing means lower standards are acceptable on large tasks.
Slicing works best when easy pieces replace the main outcome.
questions.explanation: Fact 8 says slicing is not an excuse to avoid the whole result. Formatting checks are a near miss when the recommendation stays blank.

questions.prompt: A task board shows Beatrice completed label cleanup, folder names, and chart colors while the report's main answer stayed blank. Which diagnosis fits best?
choices: The small pieces are too far from the larger outcome.
The small pieces can replace clarity about the final result.
The small pieces matter mainly because visible activity lowers worry.
questions.explanation: Fact 9 says small pieces need connection to the larger outcome. Finished bits can still miss if they do not move the report.

reviewCards.front: What does slice and dice mean when a task feels too large to start?
reviewCards.back: It means divide the large job into small pieces, then begin with one piece or one short work interval.

reviewCards.front: How does the Swiss cheese method weaken avoidance?
reviewCards.back: Swiss cheese means making small holes through partial starts. A paragraph, call, list, or source title gives attention a place to enter, so the large task feels less solid.

reviewCards.front: How is the salami slice method different from random small work?
reviewCards.back: A salami slice is a thin slice done in order. You complete one part, then the next, so motivation grows from finished movement.

reviewCards.front: Why can a five-minute start count as real work?
reviewCards.back: It separates beginning from finishing. The short start opens the task and lets attention touch the work before the whole job feels possible.

reviewCards.front: How would you restate visible next marker (Ch 10), then use it on today's large task?
reviewCards.back: Name the nearest point you can reach, not the whole road. On a large task, turn that marker into the first clear slice you can start now.

reviewCards.front: When does slicing become another way to avoid the frog?
reviewCards.back: It becomes avoidance when the slices no longer serve the result. Tiny tasks must still move the proposal, report, memo, call, or file forward.

implementationPlan.title: Mark the First Slice
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice turning a large task into one visible next move. Mark the First Slice by naming two possible pieces, comparing them, and choosing the one tied to the final result. The goal is to touch the frog, not arrange the plate.

ifThenPlans.context: A task feels too large to begin.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the whole task feels too large, then Mark the First Slice by writing the smallest useful piece beside the file.

ifThenPlans.context: The first slice sounds broad or cloudy.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the first slice is hard to picture, then compare two smaller options and choose the one you can see yourself doing.

ifThenPlans.context: Small pieces become safe busywork.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a slice does not move the final result, then cross it out and pick a piece that touches the real frog.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next 24 hours, at your next handoff between tasks, move one object onto a large task. Use it as the cue to Mark the First Slice and start that piece.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, ask one person to flag when your small pieces look disconnected from the result. Compare notes once, then rename one better first slice.

memorableLines.text: Small starts make big work touchable.
memorableLines.why: It turns the chapter's mechanism into a short rule.

memorableLines.why: It separates completed progress from scattered activity.
