chapters.title: Create large chunks of time
chapters.hook: Can 1 protected hour beat a whole day of scraps?
chapters.counterintuition: Despite how full your calendar looks, serious work rarely appears in the cracks. You create room for the frog by giving it a protected appointment.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before you start your next serious work block, spend 10 minutes counting the files, notes, and decisions you must reload; rehearse one sentence that protects the block.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Important work needs protected blocks, clear outcomes, and fewer restarts, so put your best time around the frog before the day spends it for you.

breakdown.fastRead:
Emilia blocks one hour for the proposal before her inbox opens. The task is not smaller, but the time around it is stronger. A protected work block is a scheduled stretch long enough to make real progress on one priority task. Big frogs need big rooms.

Treat the frog like an appointment with consequences. Name the outcome, protect the block, and tell people when you are unavailable. Scraps of time can handle scraps of work. Deep work needs a larger container.
breakdown.deepRead:
Files have a hidden cost. Each time Yvonne returns to a report, she has to find the spreadsheet, reopen the notes, remember the last choice, and rebuild the mental picture. Ten minutes vanish before the work even begins. A larger block saves that restart cost because the task stays warm in her hands.

That is why a calendar block works better than a strong intention. A blank hour can disappear into calls, messages, and small requests. A named block says what the hour is for: draft the proposal section, review the client files, write the decision memo. Work blocks need a named finish line.

Early time often protects the work best. Annabelle tries to write after routine demands are handled, but by then the day has learned how to interrupt her. When she moves the block before calls and messages, the hard task gets first claim on her best attention. She does not become less busy. She becomes less available to the wrong work at the wrong time.

Protection also needs other people to see it. If Ella has a blocked hour but answers every ping, the block is only a decoration. She needs a plain sentence: "I am on the client file until 11; send urgent items to the thread." The sentence is not rude. It tells the room how the work will get done.

The useful test is visible. Did a block get written on the calendar? Did it name one outcome? Did someone else know it was protected? If not, the idea stayed in your head, and the day can still spend the hour for you.
breakdown.fullRead:
Jenna sits in an onboarding room with one open laptop and three open tabs. The instructor asks the class to count how many times they restart the same file in one morning. Jenna marks five. None of the restarts looks dramatic. Each one just steals a small piece of the work.

That count changes the lesson. The problem is not only interruption. It is reentry. A complex task has context: files, notes, choices, facts, and a half-built mental map. When the map is broken into ten pieces, attention spends itself rebuilding instead of producing. One large block lets the map stay alive long enough to use it.

The block should match the frog. If the task is small, a small slot may be fine. A short email does not need a whole morning. But a proposal, plan, analysis, or hard conversation prep often needs a stretch where the mind can carry several details at once. Save your best room for your biggest frog.

There is also a social side. Ella can write "deep work" on her calendar, but if her team thinks she is free, they will keep using her as if she is free. A short note changes the setting: "I am blocked for the client files until noon; route urgent items through the project thread." The work gets a door, and the door gets a sign.

The common mistake is waiting for a large block to appear after the small work is cleared. That order rarely works. Small work breeds more small work. Messages invite replies. Calls create notes. Routine tasks can fill any space you give them. Large blocks are created, not found.

Tie the block to an outcome before it starts. "Work on strategy" is too cloudy. "Draft the three decision options" gives the hour a target. When the block ends, you can tell whether it worked. The calendar is not the win; the finished piece is.

The time-block protocol is plain: Schedule block, Define outcome, Protect from interruption, Use best energy. Emilia can check all four before she starts. No schedule means no room. No outcome means no finish. No protection means no door. Poor energy means poor work.

The overcorrection hides inside the word protected. If Blake blocks the whole week, ignores urgent handoffs, and calls every request an interruption, the method has curdled. Protected time is not a wall against responsibility. It is a fence around the work that matters most. Keep the gate, but know when to open it.

Use the block to finish meaningful work, not to look pure. Tell people what is protected, choose the task before the block begins, and count the restarts that vanish when the work gets enough room. Protected time serves the frog.

examples.title: Emilia and Blake Choose the Hour
examples.scenario: At the conference room table at 8:30, project manager Emilia opens the proposal folder and creates a 9 to 10 calendar block before her inbox loads. She treats the high-value task like a meeting with consequences and marks it protected. Across the table, Blake leaves the same proposal between four short meetings. When his first gap arrives, he is still finding the spreadsheet while Emilia is choosing the first sentence.
examples.whatToDo: Emilia treats the proposal page as an appointment with consequences, names the outcome, and starts with the file already open.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast shows why priority needs a protected appointment. A high-value task left to gaps pays a restart cost before it can produce anything.

examples.title: Annabelle Moves the First Hour
examples.scenario: On the phone before bed, Annabelle says the analysis never survives the first wave of calls and messages. Henry asks where her best hour goes. Annabelle says, "Usually to replies." Henry is quiet for a beat. "Put the frog where the world has not found you yet." Annabelle moves the analysis block before the inbox.
examples.whatToDo: Annabelle moves the analysis block before calls begin and leaves the inbox closed until the first outcome is drafted.
examples.whyItMatters: Timing can defend attention. The early block protects the hardest task before reactive demands make the calendar look already spoken for.

examples.title: Jenna Counts the Restarts
examples.scenario: In Tuesday onboarding at a training room table, new analyst Jenna is sure six short gaps can equal one work block. The instructor asks her to list the outcome and then count each restart: file, notes, decision, next step. By the fourth mark, the math feels different. The class has not learned a slogan. It has watched context vanish in pieces.
examples.whatToDo: Jenna names the outcome for the work block, counts the restarts, and sees why one protected stretch beats scattered gaps.
examples.whyItMatters: The learner's confusion makes the mechanism visible. Complex work needs continuity because files, context, decisions, and the mental model must be rebuilt after breaks.

examples.title: Yvonne Keeps the File Warm
examples.scenario: Monday, Yvonne opens the client folder three times and spends each start finding the spreadsheet, notes, decisions, and mental model. The report grows by two weak lines. Tuesday, she clears the desk, leaves the files open, and protects one block for the recommendation. The same task feels less slippery because the setup cost is paid once.
examples.whatToDo: Yvonne clears the desk, keeps the client files open, and uses one block to draft the recommendation instead of restarting the setup three times.
examples.whyItMatters: Longer blocks reduce repeated setup cost. The reader can see how one prepared stretch keeps context alive long enough to turn into output.

examples.title: Ella Names the Boundary
examples.scenario:
At the office doorway after standup, Ella has one client file under her arm and a protected block on her calendar. "If I mark it private, that should be enough," she says.
Henry shakes his head. "Private to you is invisible to us."
"So I announce it?"
"Plainly. Tell us the client file is protected until 11."
"And urgent items?"
"Send them to the thread."
examples.whatToDo: Ella tells the team the client file is protected until 11 and gives them one place for urgent items.
examples.whyItMatters: Protected time needs communication. Other people can respect the block only when they know what is closed and where true exceptions should go.

examples.title: Blake Guards the Best Block
examples.scenario: Blake sees the clean list first: approve expenses, answer three notes, tidy the agenda. They would feel good. The complex client decision memo sits below them, a high-value task with real consequences. He notices the trick. Best hour, best frog. He writes "three decision options" beside the block and leaves the easy list for later.
examples.whatToDo: Blake assigns his clearest hour to the client decision memo and names the outcome before touching the easy list.
examples.whyItMatters: The best block should serve the highest-consequence task. Otherwise protected time can become a comfortable home for low-value work.

questions.prompt: Two managers face the same complex proposal. One reserves a long block; the other works only in spare gaps. Which response fits the source idea best?
choices: The spare gaps can work if the proposal stays visible all day.
The long block can wait until smaller requests are cleared.
The long block helps because complex work needs continuity.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 says complex work benefits from uninterrupted blocks. Spare gaps repeat the error that important work can always fit between other demands.

questions.prompt: Emilia's planner has "finish proposal" in the margin, but no reserved work period. Which diagnosis follows from that entry?
choices: The task needs calendar protection, not only a strong intention.
The task can stay unblocked if its importance is obvious.
The task should wait until the day opens by itself.
questions.explanation: Fact 2 says high-value tasks require calendar protection. A margin note is a near miss because it names importance without reserving time.

questions.prompt: Jenna's training tally shows six short gaps spent reopening one report with little new text. Which reading fits the source fact?
choices: The gaps were too small for deep progress on the report.
The gaps were useful because short fragments add up evenly.
The gaps were enough because the report stayed near mind.
questions.explanation: Fact 3 says short fragments may be too small for deep progress. Adding up minutes misses the reentry cost of the report.

questions.prompt: Annabelle plans to draft her analysis after routine client calls, but three mornings in a row the calls break the work apart. Which change matches the timing lesson?
choices: Use the early block before calls and messages begin.
Use the later block once routine demands are done.
Use whichever block remains after the team settles down.
questions.explanation: Fact 4 says early blocks can protect work from later interruption. Waiting for routine demands lets those demands claim the day first.

questions.prompt: Yvonne starts the same client file three times: find files, rebuild context, remember decisions, then stop. Which cost is she paying?
choices: The setup steps keep the report familiar enough to restart.
The setup steps work like review before the real draft.
The setup steps consume the block before output begins.
questions.explanation: Fact 5 says setup costs make repeated reentry expensive. Review can sound useful, but here the repeated setup eats the time.

questions.prompt: Blake labels a protected hour "strategy," but no one can tell what should exist at the end. Which revision follows the protocol?
choices: Keep the broad label so the hour can adapt as ideas appear.
Write the specific outcome the hour should produce.
Leave the hour open so any serious task can use it.
questions.explanation: Fact 6 says a block should be tied to a specific outcome. A broad label can hide vagueness even when it sounds important.

questions.prompt: Ella blocks an hour but tells no one, then receives ordinary requests through it. Which adjustment fits the source fact?
choices: She should keep the block private so others learn its pattern.
She should tell people when the block is protected and where urgent items go.
She should answer quickly so the team still feels supported.
questions.explanation: Fact 7 says other people need to know when a block is protected. Silence leaves reasonable teammates guessing that she is available.

questions.prompt: A week plan gives every morning to minor work and looks for large blocks after the small tasks clear. What is weak in the plan?
choices: The plan depends on minor work ending with enough speed.
The plan waits for large blocks instead of creating them.
The plan protects later focus by clearing minor work first.
questions.explanation: Fact 8 says large blocks are created, not found. Waiting for minor work to clear gives small tasks first claim on the calendar.

questions.prompt: Emilia has her clearest hour free, three easy tasks ready, and a client decision memo with no options drafted. Where should the block go?
choices: Use it for the easiest tasks because they can be cleared cleanly.
Use it for any task that already has files open and ready.
Use it for the highest-consequence task that needs her best attention.
questions.explanation: Fact 9 says the best block should go to the highest-consequence task. Ease and readiness are tempting but weaker sorting rules.

reviewCards.front: What is a protected work block in plain words?
reviewCards.back: It is a scheduled stretch long enough to make real progress on one priority task, with the outcome named and interruptions held outside it.

reviewCards.front: Why treat the frog like an appointment with consequences?
reviewCards.back: A calendar block gives the high-value task protected time before small work claims it. It becomes a meeting with consequences, not a wish.

reviewCards.front: How do setup costs make fragments weaker than they look?
reviewCards.back: Each restart makes you reload files, context, decisions, and the mental model. The minutes may add up, but the progress often does not.

reviewCards.front: What should be named before a protected block begins?
reviewCards.back: Name the outcome the block should produce. A block called strategy is cloudy; a block to draft three decision options can be checked.

reviewCards.front: How would role accountability (Ch 7) change the way you protect large blocks here?
reviewCards.back: It would send your best block to the output your role is judged by, not to nearby activity. Protect the block that moves the key result area.

reviewCards.front: Why does protected time need a short message to other people?
reviewCards.back: Other people cannot respect a block they cannot see. A short note says what is protected, when you will reply, and where urgent items belong.

implementationPlan.title: Protect the Best Block
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice giving the frog a real container. Protect the Best Block by naming the outcome, choosing your clearest stretch, and telling people when that stretch is closed. The move is visible protection for important work.

ifThenPlans.context: A high-value task is only written on a to-do list.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the task matters, then Protect the Best Block by putting the outcome on the calendar before small work fills the day.

ifThenPlans.context: A task keeps making you reload files and decisions.
ifThenPlans.plan: If reentry keeps stealing the first minutes, then Protect the Best Block and keep the files, notes, and next decision together.

ifThenPlans.context: Other people keep breaking the block with ordinary requests.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the block is invisible to others, then Protect the Best Block by sending one plain sentence about when you will reply.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next 24 hours, before each important task, count the files, notes, messages, and decisions you must reload. Use the highest count to name the task that needs one larger block.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, change one thing in your setup: keep one clear surface or folder for the frog's files only. Watch whether fewer restarts make the protected block easier to enter.

memorableLines.text: Big frogs need big rooms.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the chapter's time-block rule into a portable line.

memorableLines.text: Work blocks need a named finish line.
memorableLines.why: It keeps protected time tied to a visible outcome.

memorableLines.text: Protected time serves the frog.
memorableLines.why: It states the boundary against overprotecting time for its own sake.

chapters.title: Develop a sense of urgency
chapters.hook: Most days do not fail in the hard hours; they leak in the seconds between deciding and doing.
chapters.counterintuition: You may think urgency means a tense voice and too many open tabs. In fact, the useful version is quieter: decide, say the cue, act immediately, and keep momentum on work that matters.
chapters.tryThisNow: During your next conversation about what should happen next, write NOW on the nearest page or screen edge. If delay talk starts, replace it with: do it now, then name the first move.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Urgency is action tempo: decide, say the cue, act immediately, and keep momentum on important work before delay grows new resistance.

breakdown.fastRead:
Blair has the meeting page open and the follow-up line circled. The old move would be to copy the task into tomorrow's list. Instead, she writes do it now beside the line, opens the reply window, and types the first sentence before the room clears.

A sense of urgency is a steady action tempo. It closes the space between deciding and doing. The cue matters only when a hand moves next. Quick movement on important work can make energy appear after the start, not before it. Delay fattens resistance; movement starves it.
breakdown.deepRead:
Action tempo works because it gives hesitation less room to grow. The Urgency loop has four plain parts: Decide, Say the cue, Act immediately, Keep momentum. Decide means the task is worth moving now. Say the cue means use a short command, such as do it now, before the mind starts bargaining. Act immediately means make one visible move. Keep momentum means follow that first move while the decision is still warm.

At the public library help desk, Bailey and Hunter speak over a half-filled grant form.

"I know the next step," Bailey says. "I should send the missing question to the sponsor."

"Then say the cue," Hunter says.

"Do it now."

"Good. What moves?"

Bailey slides the form closer and writes the sponsor's email at the top. The grant is not done. What matters is that the decision has not cooled into another open loop.

Many people wait for the right feeling first. That order is costly. A task can feel heavy while it is untouched and lighter once the first line exists. Calm speed starts with a clear task. This is not frantic multitasking. It is quick movement on one important task before easier work steals the opening.

Fast follow-up keeps the decision alive. If a meeting ends with a next step, send the note while the names and reason are still fresh. If a call creates a hard task, write the first line before the call fades. The energy often follows the motion.
breakdown.fullRead:
Hunter has three replies ready to clear and one sponsor question that would move the grant. Anyone watching his inbox would expect the three quick replies to win. They are visible, tidy, and easy to finish. The reveal comes when he checks the next important step. The sponsor question keeps the grant alive. The quick replies only make the inbox look calmer.

This is where urgency can be misread. Speed by itself is not the skill. A person can move fast through shallow work and still leave the frog untouched. Real urgency attaches speed to importance. The task must matter before tempo helps it.

Allison's team chat shows the same rule in a smaller channel.

Allison: "Decision made: sponsor gets the revised number."

Finn: "After lunch?"

Allison: "Do it now. Drafting the note."

Finn: "Want me to check the figure first?"

Allison: "Yes. Send the figure, then I send the note."

No speech appears in the thread. The cue turns the next step into movement while the decision still has heat.

Donovan has a different test at the call center pod. His headset comes off, and the next case is open. He starts to reach for the queue notes he likes to tidy between calls. Then he stops, puts a blue dot beside the hard follow-up, and restarts with the first sentence to the customer. The pause is the method. He catches the drift before it becomes a new routine.

Thierry's desk is quieter. A legal pad lies beside a closed laptop. At the top of the page he has written Decide, Say the cue, Act immediately, Keep momentum. Under it sits one line: "Call Allison about the missing number." His finger rests on the word now written in the margin. He has not become a louder person. He has made the next move harder to miss.

The common error is to turn urgency into a slogan. A person can say "high tempo" and still delay the one task that matters. The useful test is visible. Which object changed after the cue: the page, the file, the message, the call, the work block? If nothing moved, the word did not do its job.

The cue also needs a clean target. "Do it now" helps when the next act is small enough to name: write the first line, send the question, open the file, place the call, rank the task, protect the block. If the next act is vague, the cue becomes noise. Name the move first, then move.

The precondition is importance. Action tempo quietly assumes you have already chosen work that deserves speed. When that assumption is absent, urgency turns into busy motion. The person clears messages, polishes notes, and calls it momentum while the frog waits. Urgency should make the important task move sooner, not make lesser work feel noble.

examples.title: Blair's Now Mark
examples.scenario: Blair stands beside the returned phone call note with her pen still uncapped. One path is comfortable: copy the hard follow-up onto tomorrow's list and leave the room tidy. The other path risks a rough first sentence while the decision is still fresh. She writes do it now in the margin and weighs quiet delay against motion.
examples.whatToDo: Blair uses the internal command, opens the reply window, and writes the first follow-up sentence before the decision can cool.
examples.whyItMatters: The cue works because it interrupts hesitation with a visible move. A reader can use do it now only when the next action changes.

examples.title: Bailey Says the Cue
examples.scenario: "The grant form still feels heavy," Bailey says at the public library help desk. Hunter points to the blank sponsor line. "Name the next meaningful task." "Send the missing question." "Say it." "Do it now." "What moves?" Bailey writes the sponsor's email at the top, a quick movement that gives momentum somewhere to start.
examples.whatToDo: Bailey names the meaningful task, says do it now, and makes the first quick movement by writing the sponsor's email.
examples.whyItMatters: Momentum often starts after contact with the work. The exchange shows energy following a small move instead of arriving first.

examples.title: Hunter's Inbox Reveal
examples.scenario: Hunter's inbox has three short replies at the top, and any observer would expect those to go first. They look quick. The reveal sits lower: one fast follow-up to the sponsor will keep the grant decision alive. He pins that next step above the easy replies and drafts the first line.
examples.whatToDo: Hunter gives speed to the fast follow-up, not the easiest visible replies. He drafts the sponsor note while the decision is still useful.
examples.whyItMatters: Fast follow-up preserves decision energy. Quick work matters most when it keeps the real next step from becoming another open loop.

examples.title: Allison's Hot Thread
examples.scenario:
Allison: "Decision made: sponsor gets the revised number."
Finn: "After lunch?"
Allison: "Fast follow-up now. Drafting the note."
Finn: "I can send the figure."
Allison: "Send it here, then I follow up before the decision cools into an open loop."
examples.whatToDo: Allison turns the decision into a note right inside the thread. She asks for the figure and keeps the follow-up moving.
examples.whyItMatters: The message channel keeps the action close to the decision. Fast follow-up is easier when the next step begins before the thread drifts.

examples.title: Donovan's Blue Dot
examples.scenario: At the call center pod, Donovan's headset is off and the next case note is open. His hand reaches for the queue notes he likes to tidy between calls. He stops, marks a blue dot beside the meaningful task, says do it now, and makes a quick movement into the first customer sentence.
examples.whatToDo: Donovan marks the hard follow-up, leaves the tidy queue notes alone, and begins the customer sentence while the case is open.
examples.whyItMatters: Quick movement on the meaningful task protects momentum. The reset keeps preparation from becoming the place where urgency goes to hide.

examples.title: Thierry's Margin Cue
examples.scenario: Thierry's desk has a legal pad, a closed laptop, and one line in the margin: do it now. Above it he has written Decide, Say the cue, Act immediately, Keep momentum. The important call is named on the page. His finger rests beside now, close enough to make delay visible.
examples.whatToDo: Thierry writes the Urgency loop and the important call on the same page. He links the cue to one named action before opening lighter work.
examples.whyItMatters: Action tempo needs an important target. The margin cue helps only because it points to the call that should move first.

questions.prompt: Blair's follow-up line is circled, but the work log shows thirty minutes of harmless replies after the decision. Which reading fits action tempo?
choices: The reply streak kept Blair warm while the harder note got easier.
The inbox motion showed urgency because Blair stayed visibly busy.
The open gap let low-value replies take the place of action.
questions.explanation: Action tempo closes the space between deciding and doing. Blair stayed busy, but the circled follow-up did not move.

questions.prompt: Bailey writes do it now beside the sponsor line. One version opens a blank email; another only rereads the words. Which use of the cue matches action tempo?
choices: The reread helps if the phrase keeps the sponsor task in mind.
The cue works after Bailey feels enough energy to write cleanly.
The blank email matters because the cue broke hesitation into a move.
questions.explanation: The cue is useful when it interrupts hesitation. Rereading the words is close, but the blank email is the visible move.

questions.prompt: Bailey dreads the sponsor email, types a rough first line, and then keeps shaping the note. What changed?
choices: Her energy arrived first, so the task became safe to begin.
Her movement gave momentum something concrete to follow.
The task lost importance once the first line was easy.
questions.explanation: Momentum often follows movement. Bailey did not wait to feel ready; the rough line gave the task a place to start.

questions.prompt: Allison's thread records a decision at noon and no sponsor note by the next morning. Which repair protects the decision?
choices: Leave the decision alone so the team can return with fresh attention later.
Write a clearer summary first so no rough message leaves the team.
Draft the next important note while the reason is still fresh.
questions.explanation: Fast follow-up keeps a decision alive. Waiting for polish lets the noon choice cool into another open loop.

questions.prompt: Donovan races through queue labels while the hard customer note stays blank. What is the useful warning?
choices: Fast labeling is enough because steady speed builds the habit.
Speed belongs beside the important customer note before tidy motion.
Orderly labels should lead when they make the pod feel in control.
questions.explanation: Urgency should attach to important work. Donovan's labels look active, but the customer note is the work that needs tempo.

questions.prompt: Thierry calls himself slow by nature and sets aside the urgency loop. Which reply fits the source fact?
choices: He should wait for urgent days and use the loop only then.
He can train action tempo with a cue and one visible move.
He should trade urgency for planning because tempo is fixed.
questions.explanation: A bias for action can be trained. Thierry's cue and first move make tempo a practiced behavior, not a fixed trait.

questions.prompt: Finn postpones the sponsor note because morning may feel easier. What danger does action tempo point to?
choices: Waiting can give resistance more time to grow around the note.
Waiting can protect the note from haste while the feeling settles.
Waiting can make sense when the task remains useful tomorrow.
questions.explanation: Delay creates new resistance. Finn hopes the feeling will fade, but the pause gives the note more time to feel heavy.

questions.prompt: Hunter sees a clear task. Bailey starts the first line; Finn jumps among tabs to look urgent. Which response fits calm speed?
choices: Bailey's first line fits because clear work can move quickly.
Finn's tab switching fits because calm work needs a slower pace.
Finn's tab switching fits when visible hurry shows concern.
questions.explanation: Speed and calm can coexist when the task is clear. Bailey moves one clear line; Finn only performs hurry.

questions.prompt: Allison sends the first sponsor note quickly, then the next two linked steps move before the thread cools. What does the sequence show?
choices: High tempo helped completion by keeping each step active.
Intention carried the work once the decision was recorded.
Completion would be stronger if each step waited for a new plan.
questions.explanation: High tempo supports completion. Allison's quick linked moves keep the work alive; intention alone would not do that.

reviewCards.front: What does action tempo ask you to do after you decide a task matters?
reviewCards.back: It asks you to close the gap: decide, say the cue, act immediately, and keep momentum before delay builds new resistance.

reviewCards.front: Why is do it now more than a mood phrase?
reviewCards.back: The cue interrupts hesitation only when it triggers a visible move, such as opening the file, writing the first line, or sending the next note.

reviewCards.front: How can quick movement create the energy a person was waiting for?
reviewCards.back: Contact changes the task. Once the first line, call, or note exists, the work feels less sealed off and momentum has something to follow.

reviewCards.front: Why does fast follow-up keep a decision alive?
reviewCards.back: It moves the next step while the reason, names, and stakes are still fresh. Without it, the decision cools into another open loop.

reviewCards.front: Priority coding (Ch 6) can point to A-1. Where does that help action tempo, and when can it slow you down?
reviewCards.back: It helps by choosing which task deserves speed. It slows you down if the code becomes another pause; after A-1 is clear, move it.

reviewCards.front: When does urgency turn into shallow hurry?
reviewCards.back: It turns shallow when speed goes to lesser work. The test is whether the important task gets written, opened, sent, protected, started, or finished.

implementationPlan.title: Mark Now, Move Next
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice Mark Now, Move Next: attach a short cue to one important task and make one visible move before delay starts bargaining. The cue is not the skill by itself. It works when it changes the next line written, file opened, note sent, call placed, or task protected.

ifThenPlans.context: You catch yourself waiting after a clear decision.
ifThenPlans.plan: If hesitation starts after a decision, then mark NOW on the page and use do it now to start the first visible move.

ifThenPlans.context: You are moving fast through easy work.
ifThenPlans.plan: If speed is going to low-value work, then stop and move the cue beside the important task instead.

ifThenPlans.context: A meeting or call creates a next step.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a decision creates a next step, then send or draft the first follow-up before the decision cools.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next 24 hours, mark NOW on a page, tab, or file edge you already see. Use Mark Now, Move Next on one important task before opening easier work.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of this week, review once and name what changed about your action tempo. Note one task that moved sooner and one delay cue you will catch next week.

memorableLines.text: The cue matters only when a hand moves next.
memorableLines.why: It keeps the do it now cue tied to behavior.

memorableLines.text: Delay fattens resistance; movement starves it.
memorableLines.why: It makes the cost of waiting easy to remember.

memorableLines.text: Calm speed starts with a clear task.
memorableLines.why: It separates useful urgency from frantic multitasking.

chapters.title: Single handle every task
chapters.hook: 1 restart looks harmless, but what if it is the task tax you keep paying twice?
chapters.counterintuition: Why does a day full of work still end with the A-1 task untouched? The costly part may not be the hard task; it may be leaving and coming back again.
chapters.tryThisNow: Use tomorrow's first coffee at your usual seat as the event. Count four slow breaths, then pre-write the sentence: "I will finish my A-1 task before I open lower-value work."
chapters.keyTakeaway: Choose the A-1 task, start it first, and stay with it until it is done or parked at a clear stopping point.

breakdown.fastRead:
Marc has the A-1 folder open when a smaller message pings. His hand moves toward it, then stops. "If I answer that first, I will have to restart this report," he says. He keeps the folder open and writes the next line.

Single handling means you choose the most important task, begin, and stay with it until it is finished or at a clear stopping point. Completion proves priority. A ranked list only matters when the A-1 task survives the first tempting interruption.
breakdown.deepRead:
Restart costs hide inside switches. When Elaine leaves a hard file for a quick update, she does not return to the same place. She has to reopen the file, find the sentence, remember the aim, and talk herself back into the work.

"It was only two minutes," she tells Nicole in the stockroom doorway.

"Then why are you reading the same page again?" Nicole asks.

That is the cost. Switching makes one task ask for a new start again and again. Each return needs fresh context. Each restart gives resistance another chance to speak. The work may be the same, but the starting line keeps moving.

Single handling protects momentum by making the next behavior plain. Pick the A-1 task. Start immediately. Work without diversion. Finish or reach the defined stop. Those four steps turn priority from a list mark into a visible result.

This does not mean you never pause. If the task is too large for one sitting, name the stopping point before you leave it. Kira writes, "Draft sent to Jacqueline for price check," then closes the file. That is different from drifting away because an easier item waved from the corner.

The final frog habit is simple and stern. Do not let lower-value work vote while the A-1 file is open. Finish the frog before feeding small tasks.
breakdown.fullRead:
Adele is training new hires in the school gym when Jacques raises his hand. "What if the A-1 task takes all day?" he asks. "Do we ignore everything else until midnight?" The group laughs because the question sounds honest.

Single handling breaks when it turns into stubbornness. A hospital call, a safety issue, or a customer waiting on a hard deadline can outrank the task you chose earlier. The rule is not "never stop." The rule is "do not stop for low-value escape."

A defined stopping point keeps the rule sane. If Kira cannot finish the whole budget before the meeting, she writes the exact state of the work: draft complete, two numbers missing, next move is price check. The stop is visible. Anyone can see where to restart.

That matters because vague stopping points are disguised switches. "I will get back to this" asks your future self to rebuild the whole map. "Section two drafted; call Jacqueline for shipping number" leaves a handle on the task. The work waits in one piece instead of scattering across memory.

Lower-value work is sneakier than real interruption. It often arrives wearing a useful badge. A quick inbox sweep looks responsible. A neat file name looks tidy. A small errand looks efficient. But if the frog is still open, those jobs can become a soft exit from the task that matters.

The source idea is completion discipline. In plain words, it means you prove your priority by finishing the thing you ranked first. The proof is not stress, hours, or a busy screen. The proof is a completed task, or a clear stop that protects the next start.

Resistance often drops after sustained work begins. Marc notices this on the third paragraph of the report. The first lines feel heavy. Then the sentence path appears. The smaller message still exists, but it no longer feels urgent enough to steal the report.

This is where the earlier habits join. Clarity names the frog. Priority marks it A-1. Preparation gets the desk ready. Focus keeps lower-value work outside the door. Discipline carries the task to done.

The rule fails when the chosen task is no longer the right task. If Nicole learns that a deadline moved, or Adele gets a true emergency call from the training office, single handling should yield to the new fact. Completion discipline serves results. It should never become a reason to ignore reality.

For ordinary work, though, the test is blunt. Did you start the A-1 task first? Did you stay long enough for resistance to drop? Did you finish, or leave a written handle for the next start? Finished work beats repeated starting.

examples.title: Marc's Open Folder
examples.scenario: Marc has the A-1 task open, with the source folder under his left hand and a quick message blinking on the monitor. His fingers move to the message before he hears himself say, "I am leaving the frog again." The mistake is the live moment: he sees execution becoming list decoration, not a behavioral commitment. He turns back to the report and works until done.
examples.whatToDo: Marc names the switch out loud, keeps the A-1 folder open, and writes the next paragraph before touching the message.
examples.whyItMatters: The recovery shows priority at the moment it is tested. A ranking mark only helps when it changes the next visible act.

examples.title: Elaine's Restart Memo
examples.scenario: At the stockroom table after the Monday handoff, Elaine sends a project lead memo titled "Client File Restart Log." It reads: "Opened file, checked inbox, reopened file, found page again. Answered Nicole, reopened file, rebuilt price context." Her final line decides the rule: "No more quick switches while the A-1 file is open. Each return makes me pay for the same start twice."
examples.whatToDo: Elaine writes the restart log, names the repeated context rebuild, and protects the open A-1 file from quick switches.
examples.whyItMatters: The memo makes restart cost visible. Once the reader can see the repeated reopening, switching no longer looks free.

examples.title: Jacqueline and Nicole Finish Differently
examples.scenario: Before lunch at the shared worktable, Jacqueline clears six small tickets and says the morning was productive. The A-1 proposal still has a blank recommendation. Nicole, the reviewer, ignores the small tickets. She drafts the recommendation and marks the proposal ready. Jacqueline has activity to report. Nicole has the frog moved to a finished state.
examples.whatToDo: Nicole keeps the final frog habit tied to the recommendation paragraph and finishes that piece before touching the small tickets.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast separates motion from completion. The reader learns to ask what finished, not how busy the morning looked.

examples.title: Adele Hears the Cost
examples.scenario: "I am tired of this file," Adele says on the phone. Kira asks how many times she has rebuilt context and reopened materials today. "Four." Kira answers, "You are not tired from working; you are tired from restarting." Adele hears the resistance in the switches, then reads the next paragraph aloud so she can stay with the file.
examples.whatToDo: Adele accepts the reframe, reads the next paragraph aloud, and stays with the file until the marked section is complete.
examples.whyItMatters: The talk changes the cause she sees. If restart cost is the fatigue, another switch will not give the reader relief.

examples.title: Jacques Ranks Before Starting
examples.scenario: In the school gym training, Jacques circles three tasks and asks, "Which one do I single handle?" Adele points to the blank A-1 column on his execution sheet. "First rank them. Single handling needs the A-1 task until done." Jacques frowns, then treats the mark as a behavioral commitment and crosses out the lower-value warm-up email.
examples.whatToDo: Jacques ranks the list first, marks the grant draft A-1, and starts that task instead of the easier email.
examples.whyItMatters: The confusion is useful because it exposes the precondition. Single handling begins after priority is named, not before.

examples.title: Kira Leaves a Handle
examples.scenario: Last week, Kira shut the budget draft with only "finish later" in the margin. The restart was slow: she reopened materials, rebuilt context, and felt resistance rise. This week, at the coffee table, she writes, "Draft complete through travel; next is vendor price check." The task is not finished. The stopping point is defined, and the next start has a handle.
examples.whatToDo: Kira writes the exact stopping point and the next move before closing the budget draft.
examples.whyItMatters: A defined stop is not failure. It protects the next start when full completion is not possible yet.

questions.prompt: Marc and Elaine both open an A-1 report. Marc stays with the open file; Elaine answers every small request as it appears. Which response matches single handling?
choices: Elaine matches it because each request gets handled while it is fresh.
Elaine matches it because no one task should hold the whole work block.
Marc matches it because the chosen task stays active until completion.
questions.explanation: Single handling keeps the chosen task active until completion. The request-by-request answer treats interruption as equal to progress.

questions.prompt: Jacques has three marked tasks on his training sheet: grant draft A-1, inbox cleanup B-2, and receipt sorting C-1. Where should his first work block begin?
choices: The grant draft should begin the block because it carries the A-1 mark.
The inbox cleanup should begin the block because it is already visible.
The receipt sorting should begin the block because it can be cleared fast.
questions.explanation: The A-1 task starts first. The visible and quick tasks are plausible near misses, but they let ease outrank priority.

questions.prompt: Elaine's restart log shows one client file opened five times, with email checks between each return. Which reading fits the warning about switching?
choices: The email checks refreshed attention by changing the work often.
The repeated returns raised the cost by making context rebuild.
The five openings showed the file needed more research before drafting.
questions.explanation: The log points to restart cost: each return asks Elaine to rebuild context. The energy and research readings miss the repeated restarting.

questions.prompt: Jacqueline clears eight tiny tickets while Nicole finishes the proposal recommendation. Which result carries more weight in completion discipline?
choices: Nicole's finished recommendation carries more weight than Jacqueline's activity count.
Jacqueline's eight tickets carry more weight because the count is higher.
Both results carry equal weight because both workers stayed visibly busy.
questions.explanation: Completion matters more than activity. Jacqueline's count can look strong while the main frog remains unfinished.

questions.prompt: During Adele's call, the A-1 file is open and the next paragraph is marked. A three-minute inbox sweep appears before she finishes. What should happen next?
choices: Adele should finish the marked section before opening the inbox sweep.
Adele should clear the inbox sweep because three minutes is a small cost.
Adele should switch to the inbox sweep if it makes the desk feel lighter.
questions.explanation: Lower-value work should not interrupt the frog. The inbox sweep looks harmless because it is short, but it still pulls Adele away.

questions.prompt: Marc and Kira both feel resistance before a hard page. Marc waits for the feeling to fade; Kira works through the first page. Which pattern does the source fact support?
choices: Marc's wait fits because resistance usually rises during focused work.
Kira's first page fits because resistance often drops after sustained work.
Marc's wait fits when easier tasks can build a better mood first.
questions.explanation: Resistance often drops after sustained work begins. Waiting for the feeling to disappear puts comfort before action.

questions.prompt: Kira cannot finish the whole budget before the meeting, but she can leave one note on the draft. Which note protects the next start?
choices: I will finish this later when I have a better block.
The budget is still open, so this stop does not count.
Draft complete through travel; next is vendor price check.
questions.explanation: A defined stopping point is acceptable when full completion is impossible. Kira's specific note shows what is done and what comes next.

questions.prompt: Jacques asks Adele which of three useful tasks deserves single handling, but the list has no rank marks. What has to come before the start?
choices: He should choose the task that feels easiest to finish.
He should work on all three until one choice becomes obvious.
He should rank the list so the A-1 task is named first.
questions.explanation: Single handling requires prior prioritization. Without the A-1 mark, Jacques is just choosing by feel or activity.

questions.prompt: Adele's closing checklist puts clarity, priority, focus, and discipline beside one daily behavior. Which behavior completes that set?
choices: Preparing several possible tasks so the day stays flexible.
Choosing the A-1 task, starting it, and carrying it to done.
Moving among several tasks so each habit gets equal attention.
questions.explanation: The final habit joins earlier methods into one behavior: choose the A-1 task, start it, and carry it to done.

reviewCards.front: What does completion discipline ask you to do after you choose the A-1 task?
reviewCards.back: It asks you to begin the A-1 task and stay with it until it is finished or left at a clear stopping point.

reviewCards.front: Why do small switches make one hard task cost more?
reviewCards.back: Each switch makes you rebuild context, reopen materials, and face resistance again. The task is the same, but the start repeats.

reviewCards.front: How does the final frog habit turn daily discipline into progress?
reviewCards.back: It asks whether you finish the frog before lower-value work gets a vote. Daily discipline means A-1 moves, not just that many small tasks got attention.

reviewCards.front: When is it acceptable to stop before the whole task is finished?
reviewCards.back: Stop when full completion is not possible and the stopping point is written clearly. The note must show what is done and what comes next.

reviewCards.front: In one sentence, how does frictionless start (Ch 9) connect to completion discipline?
reviewCards.back: A frictionless start clears the desk for one task; completion discipline keeps that chosen task protected until it is finished.

reviewCards.front: What is the danger of quick lower-value work while the frog is open?
reviewCards.back: It feels useful, but it can become a soft exit from the task that matters. Quick work should wait while the A-1 task is active.

implementationPlan.title: Prewrite the Finish Line
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice protecting the A-1 task with words you have already written. Prewrite the Finish Line by naming the task, the lower-value work you will delay, and the sentence you will say when a switch tempts you. The skill is simple: start first, stay longer, and leave a clear handle if you must stop.

ifThenPlans.context: The work block begins and several tasks look useful.
ifThenPlans.plan: If several tasks call for attention, then read the A-1 line first and begin that task before opening lower-value work.

ifThenPlans.context: A quick switch looks harmless.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a quick switch tempts you, then count four slow breaths and say the prewritten line that keeps you with the open task.

ifThenPlans.context: Full completion is not possible yet.
ifThenPlans.plan: If you must stop, then write what is done and the exact next move before closing the file.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within 24 hours, during your first coffee or first commute pause, pre-write the words you will use when a quick task interrupts your A-1 work. Count four slow breaths before writing the line.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, tally each time lower-value work interrupts an open A-1 task. At week's end, read the number and pre-write one stronger refusal line.

memorableLines.why: It gives the chapter's core test in three words.

memorableLines.why: It makes the invisible price of task switching memorable.
